# Graphing Functions

## Graphing Functions

> **Spec point** — `4A`

## Graphing Functions

### How do I graph the function y = f(x)?

- A point $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x)$ if $f(a)=b$
- The **horizontal axis** is used for the **domain**

  - these are the *x-*values
- The **vertical axis** is used for the **range**

  - these are the corresponding *y-*values
- Graphing a function can involve any or all of the following **skills**

  - creating a **table of values**
  - knowing the **general shapes** and **characteristics** of different types of graphs
  - finding **axis intercepts**
  - finding **turning points** (including **maxima** and **minima**)
  - identifying **asymptotes**

### What is the difference between “draw” and “sketch”?

- '**Sketch**' questions will **not provide a detailed grid** to draw the graph on

  - A sketch is meant to show **key features** of a graph
  
    - It does not need to be perfectly to scale
    - It does not need to plot points precisely
  - When asked to **sketch** you should:
  
    - Show the correct **general shape**
    - Label any **key points** such as the intersections with the axes
    - Label the **axes**
    - Label the **graph** by giving its function or equation
- '**Draw**' questions will always** provide a detailed grid** to draw the graph on

  - A drawing of a graph is meant to be as **accurate** as possible
  - When asked to **draw** you should:
  
    - Use a **ruler** for any straight lines
    - Draw **to scale**
    - Plot any points **precisely**
    - Join points with a **straight line** or **smooth curve**
    - Label any **key points** such as the intersections with the axes
    - Label the **axes**
    - Label the **graph** by giving its function or equation

### Can my calculator help me sketch/draw a graph?

- Your **calculator** may be able to display graphs of functions

  - If so make sure you are familiar with how this feature works
- This can be useful for **checking** your work
- It can also **help** with identifying

  - the **general shape** of a graph
  - axis **intercepts**
  - **turning points** (including **maxima** and **minima**)
- But **be careful**, especially on 'show that' questions

  - Make sure key parts of an answer are **backed up by working**
  - **Marks** may depend on this

## Key Features of Graphs

> **Spec point** — `4A`

## Key Features of Graphs

### What are the key features of graphs?

You should be familiar with the following key features and know how to identify them

- Local **minima** and **maxima**

  - These are points where the graph has a minimum/maximum for a **local region**
  
    - They are the 'peaks' or 'valleys' of a graph
    - They are not necessarily the minimum or maximum for the whole graph
  - They are also called **turning points**
  - A graph can have **multiple** local minima or maxima
  - They occur where the **gradient** of the graph is equal to zero
  
    - So if you are graphing $y = f \left(x\right)$
    - Turning points will occur where  $f^{'} \left(x\right) = 0$
- **Intercepts**

  - ***y****­****­-*****intercepts** are where the graph crosses the *y*-axis
  
    - At these points  $x=0$
  - ***x-*****intercepts** are where the graph crosses the *x*-axis
  
    - At these points *y* = 0
    - These points are also called the **roots **of the function
- **Symmetry**

  - Some graphs have **lines of symmetry**
  
    - E.g. a quadratic graph has a vertical line of symmetry through its minimum or maximum point
- **Asymptotes**

  - These are lines which the graph will **get closer to** but **not cross**
  - These can be **horizontal** or **vertical**
  
    - **Exponential** graphs have horizontal asymptotes
    - **Logarithmic** graphs and graphs of **rational functions** have vertical asymptotes

![Sketching Polynomials Notes Diagram 1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/6b06e5f87da8-2-7-1-sketching-polynomials-notes-diagram-1.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - Don't forget to label the graph, the axes and key features when drawing or sketching a graph
> 
>   - Marks may depend on this
> - Your calculator may be able to help you with drawing or sketching a graph
> 
>   - But don't forget to show working, especially in a 'show that' question
> - Sketching a graph can often be useful even if a question doesn't require it

> **Worked Example**
> A function is defined by  $ f \left(x\right) = x^{2} - 4 x - 5$.
> 
> Sketch the graph $y=f(x)$.
> 
> > *Remember, 'sketch' here means we only need to show the general shape and key features*
> 
> > *This is a positive quadratic, so it is going to be a 'u-shaped' parabola*
> 
> > *Find the **y**-intercept by substituting in *$x=0$
> 
> $f \left(0\right) = \left(0\right)^{2} - 4 \left(0\right) - 5 = - 5$
> 
> > *So the **y-**intercept is *$\left(0 ,  - 5\right)$
> 
> > *The **x**-intercepts will occur when  *$y = f \left(x\right) = 0$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}x^{2} - 4 x - 5 & = & 0 \\ \left(x - 5\right) \left(x + 1\right) & = & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> $x=5,x=-1$
> 
> > *So the **x**-intercepts are *$\left(5 ,  0\right)$* and *$\left(- 1 ,  0\right)$
> 
> > *The turning point will occur when  *$f^{'} \left(x\right) = 0$
> 
> $f^{'} \left(x\right) = 2 x - 4$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 x - 4 & = & 0 \\ 2 x & = & 4 \\ x & = & 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Substitute into *$f \left(x\right)$* to find the corresponding **y-**value*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}f \left(2\right) & = & \left(2\right)^{2} - 4 \left(2\right) - 5 \\ & = & 4 - 8 - 5 \\ & = & - 9\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *So the turning point is *$\left(2 ,  - 9\right)$
> 
> > *Sketch a graph showing the correct general shape and incorporating all the key points identified above*
> *Label the graph, the axes, and the key features*
> 
> ![Graph of quadratic function](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/b8e8ed2df1e7-untitled.png)

title: Graphs of Polynomials
bodyMd:
# Graphs of Polynomials

## Quadratic Functions & Graphs

> **Spec point** — `4A`

## Quadratic Functions & Graphs

### What are the key features of quadratic graphs?

- A **quadratic** graph can be written in the form $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$ where $a\neq0$
- The shape of the graph is known as a **parabola**
- The value of *a* affects the shape of the curve

  - If *a *is **positive** the shape is **'u-shaped'** ∪
  - If *a *is **negative** the shape is **'upside down u-shaped'** ∩
- The ***y*****-intercept** is at the point (0, *c*)
- The **roots** are the solutions to $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$

  - These are also known as the ***x*****-intercepts** or **zeroes**
  - They can be found by
  
    - **Factorising**
    - **Quadratic formula**
    - **Completing the square**
    - Your **calculator** may also be able to find these for you
  - There can be **0, 1 or 2** *x-*intercepts
  
    - This is determined by the value of the **discriminant**
- There is an **axis of symmetry** at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$

  - If there are two *x*-intercepts then the axis of symmetry goes through the **midpoint** between them
- The **vertex** lies on the axis of symmetry

  - It can be found by **completing the square**
  - The *x*-coordinate is $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$
  - The *y*-coordinate can be found by calculating *y *when $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$
  - If *a* is **positive** then the vertex is the **minimum point**
  - If *a* is **negative** then the vertex is the **maximum point**

![Graphs of a quadratic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/6d7f5c08bdf4-2-2-1-quadratic-graphs-notes-diagram-1.png)

![Key features of a quadratic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/0c0634c9fa61-2-2-1-quadratic-graphs-notes-diagram-2.png)

### What are the equations of a quadratic function?

- $f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$

  - This is the **general form**
  - It clearly shows the *y*-intercept (0, *c*)
  - You can find the axis of symmetry by $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$
- $f(x)=a(x-p)(x-q)$

  - This is the **factorised form**
  - It clearly shows the roots (*p*, 0) & (*q*, 0)
  - You can find the axis of symmetry by $x=\frac{p+q}{2}$
- $f(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k$

  - This is the **vertex form** (or **completed square form**)
  - It clearly shows the vertex (*h*, *k*)
  - The axis of symmetry is therefore $x=h$
  - It clearly shows how the function can be transformed from the graph of $y=x^{2}$
  
    - Vertical stretch by scale factor ­*a*
    - Translation by vector $\begin{pmatrix} h \\ k \end{pmatrix}$

### How do I find an equation of a quadratic?

- If you have the **roots** *x *= *p *and *x* = *q*...

  - Write in **factorised form** $y=a(x-p)(x-q)$
  - You will need a third point to find the value of *a*
- If you have the **vertex** (*h*, *k*) then...

  - Write in **vertex form **$y=a(x-h)^{2}+k$
  - You will need a second point to find the value of *a*
- If you have **three random points** (*x*<sub>*1*</sub>*, y*<sub>*1*</sub>), (*x*<sub>*2*</sub>*, y*<sub>*2*</sub>) & (*x*<sub>*3*</sub>*, y*<sub>*3*</sub>) then...

  - Write in the **general form** $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$
  - Substitute the three points into the equation
  - Form and solve a system of three linear equations to find the values of *a*, *b *& *c*

> **Exam Hint**
> - Your calculator may be able to find the roots and turning point of a quadratic function
> 
>   - Even on a 'show that' question this can be used to check your answers

> **Worked Example**
> The diagram below shows the graph of $y=f(x)$, where $f(x)$ is a quadratic function.
> 
> The vertex and the intercept with the $y$-axis have been labelled.
> 
> ![2-2-1-ib-aa-sl-we-image](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/a5b66978304a-2-2-1-ib-aa-sl-we-image.png)
> 
> Find an expression for $y=f(x)$.
> 
> *Method 1*
> 
> *Since we know the vertex (turning point), it will be easiest to start with the completed square version of the equation *
> *This is  *$f(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k$*,  where the vertex is at *$\left(h ,  k\right)$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}f \left(x\right) & = & a \left(x - \left(- 1\right)\right)^{2} + 8 \\ & = & a \left(x + 1\right)^{2} + 8\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *We also know the curve *$y = f \left(x\right)$* goes through (0, 6)*
> *Put those coordinates into the equation and solve for *$a$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}6 & = & a \left(0 + 1\right)^{2} + 8 \\ 6 & = & a + 8 \\ a & = & - 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Substitute *$a=-2$* into the expression for *$f \left(x\right)$
> *Expand the brackets and rearrange into the form required*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}f \left(x\right) & = & - 2 \left(x + 1\right)^{2} + 8 \\ & = & - 2 \left(x^{2} + 2 x + 1\right) + 8 \\ & = & - 2 x^{2} - 4 x - 2 + 8\end{aligned}$
> 
> $f(x)=-2x^{2}-4x+6$
> 
> > *Method** **2*
> 
> *It is also possible to start with the *$y=ax^{2}+bx+c$* form*
> *Because the **y-**intercept is (0, 6) we know that *$c=6$
> 
> *Goes through *$\left(0 ,  6\right)$* means  *$f \left(x\right) = a x^{2} + b x + 6$
> 
> > *It also goes through (-1, 8)*
> *Substitute those coordinates into the equation of *$y = f \left(x\right)$
> 
> *Goes through *$\left(- 1 ,  8\right)$* means*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}8 & = & a \left(- 1\right)^{2} + b \left(- 1\right) + 6 \\ 8 & = & a - b + 6 \\ a - b & = & 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *We need one more piece of information*
> *You may remember that the turning point lies on the line  *$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$
> *If not, then use the fact that the **x-**coordinate of the turning point satisfies  *$f^{'} \left(x\right) = 0$
> 
> *Turning point at *$\left(- 1 ,  8\right)$* means**  *$f^{'} \left(- 1\right) = 0$
> 
> > *Differentiate to find *$f^{'} \left(x\right)$
> *Then solve *$f^{'} \left(- 1\right) = 0$* to find another equation with *$a$*and *$b$
> 
> $f^{'} \left(x\right) = 2 a x + b$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 a \left(- 1\right) + b & = & 0 \\ - 2 a + b & = & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *We now have two simultaneous equations that we can solve to find *$a$* and *$b$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}a - b & = & 2 \text{   } \left[1\right] \\ - 2 a + b & = & 0 \text{   } \left[2\right]\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Add [1] and [2] together to eliminate *$b$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}- a & = & 2 \\ a & = & - 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Substitute into [2] and solve to find *$b$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}- 2 \left(- 2\right) + b & = & 0 \\ 4 + b & = & 0 \\ b & = & - 4\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Write final answer in form requested*
> 
> $f(x)=-2x^{2}-4x+6$

## Cubic Functions & Graphs

> **Spec point** — `4A`

## Cubic Functions & Graphs

### What are the key features of cubic graphs?

- A **cubic **graph can be written in the form  $y=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d$  where $a\neq0$
- When asked to consider the **equation** of a cubic and its **graph**, think about the following

  - ***y****-*axis intercept
  
    - This occurs at  $\left(0 ,  d\right)$
  - ***x****-*axis intercepts (**roots**)
  
    - *x-*coordinates are the solutions to  $ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0$
  - **turning points** (**maximum** and/or **minimum**)
  
    - A cubic can have **0 or 2** turning points
    - *x-*coordinates are the solutions to  $3ax^{2}+2bx+c=0$
    - these are when the derivative of $ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d$ equals 0
  - The value of $a$ affects the shape of the curve
  
    - If $a$ is **positive** the ends of the curve will go 'down on the left and up on the right'
    - If $a$ is **negative** the ends of the curve will go 'up on the left and down on the right'

![Key features of a cubic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/6b06e5f87da8-2-7-1-sketching-polynomials-notes-diagram-1.png)

### How do I sketch the graph of a cubic?

- **STEP 1**       
Find the ***y****-*axis intercept by setting ***x***** = 0**
- **STEP 2**
Find the ***x***-axis intercepts (roots) by setting ***y***** = 0*** *

  - This may require **factorising** the cubic
- **STEP 3**
Consider the shape and “start”/”end” of the graph

  - a **positive** **cubic** graph starts in third quadrant (“bottom left”) and ends in first quadrant (“top right”)
  - a **negative cubic **graph starts in second quadrant (“top left”) and ends in fourth quadrant (“bottom right”)
- **STEP 4**
Consider where any **turning points** should go

  - **Differentiate** the equation of the curve and set equal to zero
- **STEP 5**
Draw with a **smooth** curve (this takes practice!)

![Steps to sketch a cubic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/d213c28c6956-2-7-1-sketching-polynomials-notes-diagram-2.png)

> **Worked Example**
> Consider the function  $f \left(x\right) = - x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x$,  where $b$ and $c$ are constants.
> 
> The graph of  $y = f \left(x\right)$  has two turning points, the $x$-coordinates of which are $1$ and $3$.
> 
> (a) Find the values of $b$ and $c$.
> 
> > *The turning points occur when *$f^{'} \left(x\right) = 0$
> 
> > *Start by differentiating to find *$f^{'} \left(x\right)$
> 
> $f^{'} \left(x\right) = - 3 x^{2} + 2 b x + c$
> 
> > *That is equal to 0 when *$x=1$* and when *$x=3$
> 
> > *Substitute those values in to find two equations in *$b$* and *$c$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}- 3 \left(1\right)^{2} + 2 b \left(1\right) + c & = & 0 \\ - 3 + 2 b + c & = & 0 \\ 2 b + c & = & 3\end{aligned}$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}- 3 \left(3\right)^{2} + 2 b \left(3\right) + c & = & 0 \\ - 27 + 6 b + c & = & 0 \\ 6 b + c & = & 27\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Those are simultaneous equations in *$b$* and *$c$
> *Subtract the first from the second to eliminate *$c$* and find *$b$
> *Then substitute that value into either equation to find *$c$
> 
> $b=6c=-9$
> 
> (b) Sketch the graph of $y = f \left(x\right)$.
> 
> > *There is no constant term in *$f \left(x\right)$*, so the **y**-intercept will be 0*
> 
> > *Substitute the **x**-coordinates of the turning points into *$f \left(x\right)$* to find the corresponding **y**-coordinates*
> 
> > * *
> 
> $- ( 1 ) ^{3} + 6 ( 1 ) ^{2} - 9 ( 1 ) = - 1 + 6 - 9 = - 4$
> 
$> - ( 3 ) ^{3} + 6 ( 3 ) ^{2} - 9 ( 3 ) = - 27 + 54 - 27 = 0$
> 
> > *So the turning points are at  *$\left(1 ,  - 4\right)$* and *$\left(3 ,  0\right)$
> 
> > *Find the **x-**intercepts by solving *$f \left(x\right) = 0$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}- x^{3} + 6 x^{2} - 9 x & = & 0 \\ - x^{3} \left(x^{2} - 6 x + 9\right) & = & 0 \\ - x^{3} \left(x - 3\right)^{2} & = & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> $x=0,x=3$
> 
> > *So the **x-**intercepts are *$\left(0 ,  0\right)$* and *$\left(3 ,  0\right)$
> *Note that the first is also the **y-**intercept. and the second is also a turning point*
> 
> > *Finally consider the shape of the curve*
> *It's a 'negative cubic', so it's going to be 'up on the left and down on the right'*
> *Draw a smooth curve incorporating all these features*
> *Label the turning points and intercepts*
> 
> ![Graph of cubic function](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/9ba3fa3a78e3-yq-ce2dp-picture1.png)

title: Graphs of Rational Functions
bodyMd:
# Graphs of Rational Functions

## Linear Rational Functions & Graphs

> **Spec point** — `4A`

## Linear Rational Functions & Graphs

### What is a linear rational function?

- A **(linear)** **rational function** is of the form  $f(x)=\frac{ax+b}{cx+d},x\neq-\frac{d}{c}$
- Its **domain** is the set of **all real values except ** $-\frac{d}{c}$

  - Because  $x=-\frac{d}{c}$  would make the denominator zero
- Its **range** is the set of **all real values except **$\frac{a}{c}$

  - Because there's no value of $x$ for which  $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}=\frac{a}{c}$
- The **reciprocal function  **$f \left(x\right) = \frac{1}{x}$** ** is a **special case** of a rational function

### What are the key features of linear rational graphs?

- The graph has a ***y*****-intercept** at $(0,\frac{b}{d})$ provided $d\neq0$

  - The is found by substituting $x=0$
- The graph has **one *****x-*****intercept** at $(-\frac{b}{a},0)$ provided $a\neq0$

  - This is found by setting the numerator equal to zero and solving the equation
- The graph has **two asymptotes**

  - A **horizontal** asymptote: $y=\frac{a}{c}$
  
    - This is the **limiting value** when the value of *x *gets very large in the positive or negative direction
  - A **vertical** asymptote: $x=-\frac{d}{c}$
  
    - This is the value that causes the **denominator to be zero**
- The graph **does not have any minimum or maximum points**
- If you are asked to **sketch or draw** a rational graph:

  - Give the **coordinates** of any **intercepts** with the axes
  - Give the **equations** of the **asymptotes**

> **Exam Hint**
> - A horizontal line should only intersect this type of graph once at most
> - The only horizontal line that should not intersect the graph is the horizontal asymptote
> 
>   - This can be used to check your sketch in an exam

> **Worked Example**
> The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\frac{10-5x}{x+2}$ for $x\neq-2$.
> 
> (a) Write down the equations of the horizontal and vertical asymptotes of the graph of $y = f \left(x\right)$.
> 
> > *The horizontal asymptote is the limiting value as **x** becomes very large in the positive or negative direction*
> 
> > *When that happens, the '10' in the numerator and '2' in the denominator no longer affect the value of the function much *
> 
> *For large values of *$x$
> 
> $f \left(x\right) \approx \frac{- 5 x}{x} = - 5$
> 
> > *That means the horizontal asymptote will be at  *$y=-5$
> 
> **Final answer:** **Horizontal asymptote:  **$y=-5$
> 
> > *The vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator becomes zero*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}x + 2 & = & 0 \\ x & = & - 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> **Final answer:** **Vertical asymptote:  **$x=-2$
> 
> (b) Find the coordinates of the intercepts of the graph of $ y = f \left(x\right)$ with the coordinate axes.
> 
> > *The **y-**intercept occurs when *$x=0$
> 
> $f \left(0\right) = \frac{10 - 5 \left(0\right)}{\left(0\right) + 2} = \frac{10}{2} = 5$
> 
> **Final answer:** **y-****intercept:  **$(0,5)$
> 
> > *The **x-**intercept occurs when *$y = f \left(x\right) = 0$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}\frac{10 - 5 x}{x + 2} & = & 0 \\ 10 - 5 x & = & 0 \\ 5 x & = & 10 \\ x & = & 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> **Final answer:** **x-****intercept:  **$(2,0)$
> 
> (c) Sketch the graph of  $y = f \left(x\right)$.
> 
> > *Don't forget to include (and label) the asymptotes, and to label the axis intercepts*
> 
> ![graph of rational function](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/7482fcdcdeda-graph-of-rational-function.png)

title: Solving Equations Graphically
bodyMd:
# Solving Equations Graphically

## Solving Equations Graphically

> **Spec point** — `4B`

## Solving Equations Graphically

### How can I solve equations graphically?

- A **graph** can be used to to help solve an equation like $f(x)=g(x)$

  - **Draw the graphs** of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$
  - The **solutions** are the ***x*****-coordinates** of the points of **intersection**
- This can be used when an equation is difficult or impossible to solve **algebraically**

  - The solutions found will usually be **approximations** rather than exact answers
  - The more **accurate** the graph, the more accurate the approximation

### How can I estimate a solution by drawing a line on a graph?

- An exam question my ask you to **estimate a solution** by drawing a 'suitable' (or 'appropriate') **straight line** on a graph
- Often this will be a **horizontal** line

  - For example solving $f \left(x\right) = k$ for some constant $k$
  
    - On a graph of $y = f \left(x\right)$, draw the line $y=k$
    - The solutions are the ***x-*****coordinates** of any points of intersection
  - Finding **roots** by seeing where a graph crosses the *x*-axis is a special case of this
  
    - The *x-*axis is the horizontal line with equation  $y=0$
- Sometimes it will be the line  $y=x$

  - Draw this on the graph of $y = f \left(x\right)$ to find the solution(s) of $f \left(x\right) = x$
- But sometimes determining the line to draw will be **more challenging**

  - For example, 'By drawing an appropriate straight line on the graph of $y=3+2e^{-2x}$, estimate the root of the equation  $ln \left(x - 3\right)^{3} = - 6 x$'
  - We need to **rewrite** the equation in the form  $g \left(x\right) = 3 + 2 e^{- 2 x}$, where $y = g \left(x\right)$ is the equation of a straight line
  - Take the **exponential** of both sides ('exp cancels log')
  
    - $\left(x - 3\right)^{3} = e^{- 6 x}$
  - Take the **cube root** of both sides
  
    - $x-3=e^{-2x}$
  - **Multiply** both sides by 2
  
    - $2x-6=2e^{-2x}$
  - **Add** 3 to both sides
  
    - $2x-3=3+2e^{-2x}$
  - That equation is **equivalent** to  $ln \left(x - 3\right)^{3} = - 6 x$
  
    - it will have the same solutions
  - So we need to **draw the line**  $y=2x-3$  on the graph of  $y=3+2e^{-2x}$
  
    - the* ****x-*****coordinates** of the points of intersection will give the solution(s) for  $2x-3=3+2e^{-2x}$
    - But those are the **same** as the solution(s) for  $ln \left(x - 3\right)^{3} = - 6 x$

> **Exam Hint**
> - Be extra careful when drawing graphs on 'estimate solutions by using a graph' questions
> 
>   - The accuracy of your answer will depend on the accuracy of your drawing
>   - Use a ruler for straight lines

> **Worked Example**
> A graph of  $y = 2^{\left(\frac{x}{3} + 1\right)} - 1$  in the interval  $0\leqx\leq6$  is shown in the following diagram
> 
> ![Graph of exponential function](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/2d75892b9aeb-qb9hr5gw-picture1.png)
> 
> By drawing a suitable straight line on the grid, show that the equation  $log_{2} \left(3 x - 1\right)^{2} - \frac{2}{3} x = 2$  has a root in the interval  $0\leqx\leq6$, and obtain an estimate for the value of that root.
> 
> > *Be careful here – we cannot just draw the horizontal line *$y=2$
> *That would only work if we had the graph of  *$y = log_{2} \left(3 x - 1\right)^{2} - \frac{2}{3} x$
> 
> > *Instead we must work on rearranging the equation*
> *Start by getting the logarithm alone on the left-hand side*
> 
> $log_{2} \left(3 x - 1\right)^{2} = \frac{2}{3} x + 2$
> 
> > *Use laws of logarithms to bring the power down in front of the logarithm*
> *Then divide both sides of the equation by 2*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 log_{2} \left(3 x - 1\right) & = & \frac{2}{3} x + 2 \\ log_{2} \left(3 x - 1\right) & = & \frac{x}{3} + 1\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Now take both sides to the power of 2*
> *This will cancel the logarithm on the left-hand side ('exp cancels log')*
> 
> $3 x - 1 = 2^{\left(\frac{x}{3} + 1\right)}$
> 
> > *Finally subtract 1 from both sides*
> 
> $3 x - 2 = 2^{\left(\frac{x}{3} + 1\right)} - 1$
> 
> > *Now the right-hand side is the function that is graphed on the diagram*
> *So we need to draw the straight line  *$y=3x-2$
> *We can estimate the root by considering the **x-**coordinate of the point of intersection*
> 
> ![Solution graph for question](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/276d6f8c5dc3-rvnd1ehm-picture2.png)
> 
> **Final answer:** **root:  **$x\approx1.2$

title: Algebraic Division
bodyMd:
# Algebraic Division

## Algebraic Division

> **Spec point** — `3A`

## Algebraic Division

### What is algebraic division?

- **Algebraic division **(or **polynomial division**) is a method for **splitting polynomials** into **factor pairs** (with or without an accompanying **remainder** term)

  - On the exam you will use it to **factorise** polynomials, or to help **simplify** algebraic fractions

![2.5.2 Polynomial Division What Is, Edexcel A Level Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/edc2472a77e9-2-5-2-polynomial-division-what-is.png)

- Remember that a **polynomial** is an algebraic expression consisting of

  - a **finite** number of terms
  - with **non-negative integer indices** only

![2.5.2 Polynomial not polynomial, Edexcel A Level Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/daaf557aa4e8-2-5-2-polynomial-not-polynomial.png)

### How do I perform algebraic division?

- The **method** used for **algebraic division** is just like the method used to divide **regular numbers**

  - i.e. the **long division** method (sometimes called '**bus stop division**')

![2.5.2 Bus Stop Div, Edexcel A Level Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/9d0bd1f16fe1-2-5-2-bus-stop-div.png)

- On your exam the polynomial you are **dividing** (known as the **dividend**) will normally be of **degree 3 or 4**

  - That is, with powers of *x*  up to ***x***<sup>**3**</sup>* *or ***x***<sup>***4***</sup>
- The term you are **dividing by** (known as the **divisor**) will be a **linear** term

  - Usually in the form **(*****x***** ± *****a*****)**
  - But possibly in the form **(a*****x***** ± *****b*****)**
- The answer to an algebraic division question is built up **term by term**

  - Working **downwards** in powers of the variable (usually ***x***)

- Start with the **highest power term** of the answer

  - Write out this **multiplied** by the divisor and **subtract**

![2.5.2 Polynomial Division Illustration_1, Edexcel A Level Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/184ee257f78d-2-5-2-polynomial-division-illustration-1.png)

- Continue the process for each **decreasing power term**

  - **multiplying** by the divisor and **subtracting** each time

![2.5.2 Polynomial Division Illustration_2, Edexcel A Level Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/6d7bfd4a05ba-2-5-2-polynomial-division-illustration-2.png)

- **Continue** until you are left only with a **number** (with no ***x***'s)

  - That number is the **remainder**
  - If the divisor is a **factor** of the polynomial, the remainder will be **zero**

![2.5.2 Polynomial Division Illustration_3, Edexcel A Level Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/26f12e7cb5fd-2-5-2-polynomial-division-illustration-3.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - Don't rush when doing algebraic division
> 
>   - Finding and fixing a mistake can take longer than taking the time to do it right the first time!
> 
> - Before starting algebraic division make sure it is really necessary
> 
>   - For example, if all you need is the remainder then using the **remainder theorem** would be quicker

> **Worked Example**
> ![2.5.2 Polynomial Division Example, Edexcel A Level Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/123eac1bc519-2-5-2-polynomial-division-example.png)

title: Factor & Remainder Theorems
bodyMd:
# Factor & Remainder Theorems

## Factor Theorem

> **Spec point** — `3B`

## Factor Theorem

### What is the factor theorem?

- The **factor theorem** is used to find the linear **factors** of a function

  - This is closely related to finding the **roots** (or **solutions**) of a function or equation
- For a function $f \left(x\right)$, the **factor theorem** tells us that

  - If  $f \left(a\right) = 0$, then $\left(x - a\right)$ is a factor of $f \left(x\right)$
  - If $\left(x - a\right)$ is a factor of $f \left(x\right)$, then  $f \left(a\right) = 0$

### How do I use the factor theorem?

- Consider the  function $f \left(x\right)$ where $\left(x - a\right)$ is a factor

  - Then by the factor theorem we know that $f \left(a\right) = 0$
  
    - I.e., $x=a$ is a solution to the equation  $f \left(x\right) = 0$
- Or consider the function $f \left(x\right)$ where $f \left(a\right) = 0$

  - Then by the factor theorem we know  that $\left(x - a\right)$ is a factor of $f \left(x\right)$
  - Therefore  $f(x)=(x-a)\timesQ(x)$
  
    - where $Q \left(x\right)$ is a function that is also a factor of $f \left(x\right)$
  - Hence  $\frac{f(x)}{x-a}=Q(x)$
  
    - I.e. $Q \left(x\right)$ is the **quotient** when $f \left(x\right)$ is divided by $\left(x - a\right)$
    - And the **remainder** is equal to zero
- If the linear factor has a **coefficient of *****x**** *(other than 1) you must first factorise out the coefficient

  - For the linear factor  $\left(b x  –  c\right)  = b \left(x - \frac{c}{b}\right)$
  
    - $f \left(\frac{c}{b}\right) = 0$
    - $f \left(x\right) = b \left(x - \frac{c}{b}\right) \times Q \left(x\right)$

> **Exam Hint**
> - Be careful with the minus sign in a factor $\left(x - a\right)$
> 
>   - That means $a$ is a solution to $f \left(x\right) = 0$, not $-a$ !
> - If you are looking for **integer** solutions to $f \left(x\right) = 0$  (where $f \left(x\right)$ is a polynomial)
> 
>   - those solutions will always be factors of the constant term in $f \left(x\right)$

> **Worked Example**
> a) Consider the function$f(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+2$. Given that $x=2$ is a solution to the equation $f \left(x\right) = 0$, write down a linear factor of $f \left(x\right)$.
> 
> *By the factor theorem, if  *$f \left(a\right) = 0$* then *$\left(x - a\right)$* is a factor of *$f \left(x\right)$
> 
> > $x-2$* *
> 
> b) Use the factor theorem to determine whether $\left(x + 1\right)$ is a factor of $g(x)=2x^{3}+3x^{2}-x+5$.
> 
> > *By the factor theorem, *$\left(x - a\right)$* can only be a factor of *$g \left(x\right)$* if  *$g \left(a\right) = 0$*.*
> 
> > *But be careful – here *$a$* is equal to *$-1$*, not *$1$
> 
> **Final answer:** $\begin{aligned}g \left(- 1\right) & = & 2 \left(- 1\right)^{3} + 3 \left(- 1\right)^{2} - \left(- 1\right) + 5 \\ & = & - 2 + 3 + 1 + 5 \\ & = & 7\end{aligned}$
> $g(-1)\neq0$**, so **$(x+1)$** is not a factor of **$g(x)$
> 
> c) It is given that $\left(2 x - 3\right)$ is a factor of $ h \left(x\right) = 2 x^{3} - b x^{2} + 7 x - 6$. Find the value of $b$.
> 
> > $\left(2 x - 3\right) = 2 \left(x - \frac{3}{2}\right)$*,  so *$\left(x - \frac{3}{2}\right)$* is a factor of *$h \left(x\right)$*.*
> 
> > *Therefore by the factor theorem, *$h \left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = 0$*.*
> 
> $\begin{aligned} 2 \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{3} - b \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{2} + 7 \left(\frac{3}{2}\right) - 6 & = & 0 \\ \frac{27}{4} - \frac{9}{4} b + \frac{21}{2} - 6 & = & 0 \\ \frac{45}{4} - \frac{9}{4} b & = & 0 \\ \frac{9}{4} b & = & \frac{45}{4} \\ b & = & \frac{4}{9} \times \frac{45}{4}\end{aligned}$
> 
> $b=5$

## Remainder Theorem

> **Spec point** — `3B`

## Remainder Theorem

### What is the remainder theorem?

- The **remainder theorem** is used to find the remainder when we divide a **polynomial** function by a linear function
- When a polynomial function $f \left(x\right)$ is divided by a linear function $\left(x - a\right)$, the value of the **remainder **$R$ is given by $f \left(a\right) = R$

  - Note, if $f \left(a\right) = 0$ then $\left(x - a\right)$ is a factor of $f \left(x\right)$; this is the factor theorem

### How do I use the remainder theorem?

- Consider a polynomial function $f \left(x\right)$ and a linear function  $\left(x - a\right)$

  - $\frac{f \left(x\right)}{\left(x - a\right)} = Q \left(x\right) + \frac{R}{\left(x - a\right)}$
  
    - $Q \left(x\right)$ is the **quotient** (also a polynomial function)
    - $R$ is the **remainder **(a real number)
  - This may also be written as $f \left(x\right) = Q \left(x\right) \times \left(x - a\right) + R$
  - The **remainder theorem** tells us that  $R = f \left(a\right)$
  
    - I.e. we don't need to do the **algebraic division** to find the remainder!
- If the linear factor has a **coefficient of *****x*** (other than 1) then you must first factorise out the coefficient

  - For the linear function $\left(b x - c\right) = b \left(x - \frac{c}{b}\right)$
  
    - $R = f \left(\frac{c}{b}\right)$

> **Exam Hint**
> - Be careful with the minus sign in $\left(x - a\right)$
> 
>   - You need to put $a$ into $f \left(x\right)$ to find the remainder, not $-a$!

> **Worked Example**
> a) Find the remainder when the function $f \left(x\right) = 2 x^{4} - 2 x^{3} - x^{2} - 3 x + 1$ is divided by $\left(x - 2\right)$.
> 
> > *We're dividing by *$\left(x - a\right) = \left(x - 2\right)$
> 
> > *So *$a=2$
> 
> > *By the remainder theorem the remainder will be *
> 
> $\begin{aligned}f \left(2\right) & = & 2 \left(2\right)^{4} - 2 \left(2\right)^{3} - \left(2\right)^{2} - 3 \left(2\right) + 1 \\ & = & 32 - 16 - 4 - 6 + 1 \\ & = & 7\end{aligned}$
> 
> **Final answer:** **Remainder = 7**
> 
> b) The remainder when $g \left(x\right) = 2 x^{3} + x^{2} + b x + 1$ is divided by $\left(2 x + 1\right)$ is 3.  Find the value of $b$.
> 
> $\left(2 x + 1\right) = 2 \left(x + \frac{1}{2}\right) = 2 \left(x - \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)\right)$
> 
> > *So here the value of *$a$* to use is  *$-\frac{1}{2}$
> 
> > *By the remainder theorem the remainder will be equal to *$g \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} + \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} + b \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) + 1 & = & 3 \\ - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} - \frac{b}{2} + 1 & = & 3 \\ - \frac{b}{2} & = & 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> $b=-4$

title: Simultaneous Equations
bodyMd:
# Simultaneous Equations

## Linear Simultaneous Equations

> **Spec point** — `3C`

## Linear Simultaneous Equations

### What are linear simultaneous equations?

- When there are two unknowns (say ***x***** and *****y***) in a problem, we need two equations to be able to find them both: these are called simultaneous equations

  - you solve **two **equations to find **two **unknowns, *x* and *y*
  
    - for example, 3*x* + 2*y* = 11 and 2*x* - *y* = 5
    - the solutions are *x* = 3 and *y* = 1
- If they just have* x* and *y* in them (no *x*<sup>2</sup> or *y*<sup>2</sup> or *xy* etc) then they are **linear** simultaneous equations

### How do I solve linear simultaneous equations by elimination?

- "Elimination" completely removes one of the variables, *x *or *y*
- To eliminate the *x*'s from 3*x* + 2*y* = 11 and 2*x* - *y* = 5

  - Multiply every term in the first equation by 2
  
    - 6*x* + 4*y* = 22
  - Multiply every term in the second equation by 3
  
    - 6*x* - 3*y* = 15
  - **Subtract** the second result from the first to eliminate the 6x's
  
    - leaving 4*y* - (-3*y*) = 22 - 15, i.e. 7*y* = 7
  - Solve to find *y* (*y* = 1) then substitute *y* = 1 back into either original equation to find *x* (*x* = 3)
- Alternatively, to eliminate the *y*'s from 3*x* + 2*y* = 11 and 2*x* - *y* = 5

  - Multiply every term in the second equation by 2
  
    - 4*x* - 2*y* = 10
  - **Add** this result to the first equation to eliminate the 2*y*'s (as 2*y* + (-2*y*) = 0)
  
    - The process then continues as above
- **Check** that your final solutions satisfy both equations

### How do I solve linear simultaneous equations by substitution?

- "Substitution" means substituting one equation into the other
- Solve 3*x* + 2*y* = 11 and 2*x* - *y* = 5 by substitution

  - Rearrange one of the equation into *y* = ... (or *x* = ...)
  
    - For example, the second equation becomes *y* = 2*x* - 5
  - Substitute this into the first equation (replace all *y*'s with 2*x* - 5 in brackets)
  
    - 3*x* + 2(2*x* - 5) = 11
  - Solve this equation to find *x* (*x* = 3), then substitute *x* = 3 into *y* = 2*x* - 5 to find *y* (*y* = 1)
- **Check** that your final solutions satisfy both equations

### How do I use graphs to solve linear simultaneous equations?

- **Plot** both equations on the same set of axes

  - to do this, you can use a table of values or rearrange into *y* = *mx* + *c *if that helps
- Find where the lines **intersect** (cross over)

  - The *x* and *y  ***solutions** to the simultaneous equations are the *x- *and *y-***coordinates** of the point of **intersection**
- e.g. to solve 2*x *- *y* = 3 and 3*x* + *y* = 7 simultaneously, first plot them both (see graph)

  - find the point of intersection, (2, 1)
  - the solution is *x* = 2 and *y* = 1

![Solving Equations Graphically Notes Diagram 1, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/21072b111f5f-2-7-3-solving-equations-graphically-notes-diagra.png)

### How do I solve linear simultaneous equations from worded contexts?

![EPS Notes fig2 (1), downloadable IGCSE & GCSE Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/95b0cd4fec7a-3-8-1-eps-notes-fig2-1.png)

![EPS Notes fig2 (2), downloadable IGCSE & GCSE Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/04b4584cb569-3-8-1-eps-notes-fig2-2.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - Always check that your final solutions satisfy the original simultaneous equations - you will know immediately if you've got the right solutions or not.

> **Worked Example**
> Solve the simultaneous equations
> 
> $5x+2y=11$
> 
> $4x-3y=18$
> 
> > *Number the equations.*
> 
> > $\begin{aligned}5 x \textrm{ } + \textrm{ } 2 y \textrm{ } & = & \textrm{ } 11 \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \\ 4 x \textrm{ } - \textrm{ } 3 y \textrm{ } & = & \textrm{ } 18 \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ }\end{aligned}$$\begin{aligned} & & \left(1\right) \\ & & \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$* *
> 
> > *Make the **y**  terms equal by multiplying all parts of equation (1) by 3 and all parts of equation (2) by 2.*
> *This will give two 6**y  **terms with different signs. The question could also be done by making the **x  **terms equal by multiplying all parts of equation (1) by 4 and all parts of equation (2) by 5, and subtracting the equations.*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}15 x \textrm{ } + \textrm{ } 6 y \textrm{ } & = & \textrm{ } 33 \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \\ 8 x \textrm{ } - \textrm{ } 6 y \textrm{ } & = & \textrm{ } 36 \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ }\end{aligned}$$\begin{aligned} & & \left(3\right) \\ & & \left(4\right)\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *The 6**y**  terms have different signs, so they can be eliminated by adding equation (4) to equation (3). *
> 
> $\begin{matrix}\text{   } 15 x  +  6 y  =  33 \text{   } \\ \underline{ + \left(\text{   } 8 x  -  6 y  =  36\right) } \\ \text{   } 23 x \text{   } =  69 \end{matrix}$
> 
> > *Solve the equation to find** x  **by dividing both sides by 23.*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}x  & = &  \frac{69}{23} =  3\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Substitute **x **= 3 into either of the two original equations**.*
> 
> > $\left(1\right) \text{   }$* *$5 \left(3\right)  +  2 y  =  11$
> 
> > *Solve this equation to find** y.*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}15  +  2 y  & = &  11 \\ 2 y  & = &  11  -  15 \\ 2 y  & = &  - 4  \\ y  & = & \frac{- 4}{2}  =  - 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Substitute **x** = 3  and **y** = - 2 into the other equation to check that they are correct*
> 
> > $\begin{aligned} & & \left(2\right) \text{   }\end{aligned}$* *$\begin{aligned}4 x  -  3 y  & = &  18\end{aligned}$
> *   *$\begin{aligned}4 \left(3\right)  -  3 \left(- 2\right)  & = &  18 \\ 12  - \left(- 6\right)  & = &  18 \\ 18  & = &  18\end{aligned}$
> 
> $x=3,y=-2$

## Quadratic Simultaneous Equations

> **Spec point** — `3C`

## Quadratic Simultaneous Equations

#### What are quadratic simultaneous equations?

- When there are two unknowns (say *x* and *y *) in a problem, we need two equations to be able to find them both: these are called** simultaneous equations**
- If there is an *x*<sup>2</sup> or *y*<sup>2</sup> or *xy  *in one of the equations then they are **quadratic** (or **non-linear**) simultaneous equations

#### How do I solve quadratic simultaneous equations?

- Use the method of substitution

  - **Substitute** the** linear** equation, *y* = ... (or *x* = ...), into the quadratic equation
  
    - Do not try to substitute the quadratic equation into the linear equation
- For example solve *x*<sup>2</sup> + *y*<sup>2</sup> = 25 and *y* - 2*x* = 5

  - **Rearrange** the **linear** equation into *y *= 2*x* + 5
  - **Substitute** this into the quadratic equation, replacing all *y*'s with (2*x* + 5) in **brackets**
  
    - *x*<sup>2</sup> + (2*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> = 25
  - Expand and **solve** this **quadratic** equation (*x* = 0 and *x* = -4)
  - Substitute **each** value of *x* into the **linear** equation, *y* = 2*x* + 5, to get their value of *y*
  - Present your solutions in a way that makes it obvious which* x * belongs to which *y*
  
    - *x* = 0, *y* = 5 or *x* = -4, *y* = -3
- **Check** that your final solutions satisfy both equations

#### How do you use graphs to solve quadratic simultaneous equations?

- **Plot** both equations on the same set of axes

  - to do this, you can use a table of values (or, for straight lines, rearrange into *y* = *mx* + *c  *if it helps)
- Find where the lines **intersect** (cross over)

  - The *x * and *y  ***solutions** to the simultaneous equations are the *x- *and *y-***coordinates** of the point of **intersection**
- e.g. to solve y = *x*<sup>2</sup> + 3*x* + 1 and *y* = 2*x* + 1 simultaneously, first plot them both (see graph)

  - find the points of intersection, (-1, -1) and (0, 1)
  - the solutions are *x* = -1 and *y* = -1, or *x* = 0 and *y* = 1

![Solving Equations Graphically - Notes Diagram 4, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/d373ae6a8364-2-7-3-solving-equations-graphically-notes-diagra.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - If the quadratic resulting from substitution has
> 
>   - a **repeated root,** then the line is a **tangent** to the curve
>   - **no roots,** then the line does not intersect with the curve – or you have made a mistake!
> - When giving your final answer, make sure you indicate which *x*  and *y*  values go together
> 
>   - If you don’t make this clear you can lose marks for an otherwise correct answer.
> - Don't make the common mistake of thinking each squared term in *x*<sup>2</sup> + *y*<sup>2</sup> = 25 can be square-rooted to give *x* + *y* = 5
> 
>   - They can't, the most you can do is $\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}=\pm5$
>   - But you shouldn't be trying to make* x* or *y * the subject of this anyway!)

> **Worked Example**
> Solve the equations
> 
> $x^{2}+y^{2}=36$
> 
> $x=2y+6$
> 
> > *Number the equations.*
> 
> > $x^{2}+y^{2}=36\,x=2y+6$$( 1 )$
$> ( 2 )$* *
> 
> > *There is one quadratic equation and one linear equation so this must be done by substitution.*
> 
> > *Equation (2) is equal to *$x$* so this can be eliminated by substituting it into the *$x$* part for equation (1).*
> *Substitute *$x=2y+6$* into equation (1).*
> 
> $\left(2 y  +  6\right)^{2}  +  y^{2}  =  36$
> 
> > *Expand the brackets, remember that a bracket squared should be treated the same as double brackets.*
> 
> $( 2 y + 6 ) ( 2 y + 6 ) + y ^{2} = 36$
$> 4 y^{2} + 6 ( 2 y ) + 6 ( 2 y ) + 6 ^{2} + y^{2} = 36$
> 
> > *Simplify.*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}4 y^{2 } +  12 y  +  12 y  +  36  +  y^{2 } & = &  36 \\ 5 y^{2 } +  24 y  +  36  & = &  36\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Rearrange to form a quadratic equation that is equal to zero.*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}5 y^{2 } +  24 y  +  36  -  36  & = &  0 \\ 5 y^{2}  +  24 y  & = &  0\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Both terms contain a power of *$y$
> *So this can be factorised by taking out a common factor of *$\begin{aligned} & & y\end{aligned}$*.*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}y \left(5 y  +  24\right)  & = &  0\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Solve to find the values of *$y$*.*
> *Let each factor be equal to 0 and solve.*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}y_{1}  & = &  0 \text{   } \\ 5 y_{2}  +  24  & = &  0 \text{   } \Rightarrow \text{   } y_{2} =  - \frac{24}{5}  =  - 4 . 8\end{aligned}$
> 
> *Substitute the values of *$y$* **into one of the equations (the linear equation is easier) to find the values of *$x$*.*
>               $x_{1}  =  2 \left(0\right)  +  6  =  6 \text{   } x_{2}  =  2 \left(- \frac{24}{5}\right)  +  6  =  - 9 . 6  +  6$
> 
> **                                                                                                             **$x_{1}=6,y_{1}=0$
> *                                                                                         *$x_{2}=-3.6,y_{2}=-4.8$

title: Solving Cubic Equations
bodyMd:
# Solving Cubic Equations

## Solving Cubic Equations

> **Spec point** — `3B`

## Solving Cubic Equations

### How many real solutions can a cubic equation have?

- A **cubic equation **$ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0$** **will **always** have either **one** or **three real roots** (or **solutions**)

  - Some of these roots may be **repeated**
  - So it is possible to have one, two, or three **unique** solutions
- A cubic with **three real roots** $α$, $β$ and $γ$ can be written as a product of three **linear factors**

  - $a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d = \left(x - \alpha\right) \left(x - \beta\right) \left(x - \gamma\right)$
  
    - Any two of the factors could be multiplied together to give a **quadratic factor**
- A cubic with **one real root** $α$ can be written as the product of a **linear** and a **quadratic** factor

  - $a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d = \left(x - \alpha\right) \left(p x^{2} + q x + r\right)$
  
    - The quadratic factor will **not** have any real roots
    - So its **discriminant **$q^{2}-4pr$ will be negative

### How do I solve cubic equations?

- Suppose you have a **cubic equation** $ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0$
- An exam question will often **give** you one root

  - You may be asked to **show** that the root is a solution to the equation
  - Or you might have to **find** a root $x=α$* *by substituting values into the equation until it equals 0
  
    - Try small integer values ($1,-1,2,-2,...$)
- If you know a **root** then you know a **factor**

  - This is because of the **factor theorem**
  
    - If $x=α$ is a root, then $\left(x - \alpha\right)$ is a factor
- You can then **divide** $ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d$ by $\left(x - \alpha\right)$ to find a **quadratic factor**

  - $a x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x + d = \left(x - \alpha\right) \left(p x^{2} + q x + r\right)$
  - Use **algebraic division**, or factorise by **inspection **or by **comparing coefficients**
- Then you can find any **other roots** by solving  $px^{2}+qx+r=0$

  - If that equation has no real solutions, then $x=α$ is the **only** real solution of the cubic

> **Exam Hint**
> - Solving cubic questions may also include a graph of the cubic function
> 
>   - Remember that roots correspond to *x*-intercepts on the graph

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Show that $x=2$ is a solution to the cubic equation $2x^{3}-x^{2}-8x+4=0$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Substitute *$x=2$* into the equation*
> 
> **Final answer:** $\begin{aligned}2 \left(2\right)^{3} - \left(2\right)^{2} - 8 \left(2\right) + 4 & = & 16 - 4 - 16 + 4 = 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> **Therefore **$x=2$** is a solution**
> 
> (b) Find the other solutions to the equation.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *By the factor theorem, you know that *$\left(x - 2\right)$* is a factor of *$2x^{3}-x^{2}-8x+4$* *
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 x^{3} - x^{2} - 8 x + 4 & = & \left(x - 2\right) \left(p x^{2} + q x + r\right)\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *You can find the values of *$p$*, *$q$* and *$r$* by comparing coefficients*
> 
> - *You might also be able to do this by inspection*
> 
>   - *or else you could use algebraic division*
> - *Start by expanding the brackets*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 x^{3} - x^{2} - 8 x + 4 & = & p x^{3} + \left(q - 2 p\right) x^{2} + \left(r - 2 q\right) x - 2 r\end{aligned}$
> 
> - *The *$x^{3}$* coefficient and constant term give you *$p$* and *$r$* right away*
> 
> $2x^{3}=px^{3}\Rightarrowp=2\,\,4=-2r\Rightarrowr=-2$
> 
> - *Use either the *$x^{2}$* or *$x$* coefficients to find the value of *$q$
> 
> > $- x^{2} = \left(q - 2 p\right) x^{2}$
> * *$\begin{aligned}q - 2 p & = & - 1 \\ q - 2 \left(2\right) & = & - 1 \\ q - 4 & = & - 1 \\ q & = & 3\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Now you can write the cubic in factorised form*
> 
> $\left(x - 2\right) \left(2 x^{2} + 3 x - 2\right) = 0$
> 
> > *To find the other solutions you need to solve  *$2x^{2}+3x-2=0$
> 
> - *Any quadratic solving method would work*
> - *But it is easiest here if you can spot the factorisation*
> 
> $\left(x - 2\right) \left(x + 2\right) \left(2 x - 1\right) = 0$
> 
> - *So the other solutions are *
> 
>   - $x=-2$*,  from the factor *$\left(x + 2\right)$
>   - $x=\frac{1}{2}$*,  from the factor *$\left(2 x - 1\right) = 2 \left(x - \frac{1}{2}\right)$
> 
> $x=-2\mathrm{and}x=\frac{1}{2}$
