# Graphs of Inequalities

## Finding Regions using Inequalities

> **Spec point** — `3E`

## Finding Regions using Inequalities

### How do I draw inequalities on a graph?

- **STEP 1**
**Draw** the line (as if using “=”) for each inequality

  - Use a **solid** line for ≤ or ≥
  
    - to indicate the line **is included**
  - Use a **dashed **line for < or >
  
    - to indicate the line **is not included**
- **STEP 2**
**Decide** which side of line is wanted.

  - **Below** line if "*y* ≤ ..." or "*y* < ..."
  - **Above** line if "*y *≥ ..." or "*y* > ..."
  - To the **left** of the line if "*x* ≤ ..." or "*x* < ..."
  - To the **right** of the line if "*x *≥ ..." or "*x* > ..."
  - If unsure, use a point that's not on the line as a test
  
    - **Substitute** its *x* and *y* value into the inequality and check if the inequality is satisfied
    - This will tell you whether or not the inequality **holds true** on that side of the line
  - It's helpful to** indicate** the 'correct side' of each line on your sketch
- **STEP 3**
**Choose** the region that satisfies **all** of the inequalities

  - This is the region that is **on the correct side** of all the lines
  - The exam question will often ask you to **shade **and/or **label **the region

> **Exam Hint**
> - You can also indicate a region by shading the **unwanted** bits and leaving the region **unshaded**
> 
>   - Some students find this **easier**
>   - The mark scheme awards **full marks** for either method

> **Worked Example**
> On the axes given below show, by shading on your sketch, the region that satisfies the following three inequalities:
> 
> $3x+2y\geq12$                  $y<2x$                 $x<3$
> 
> Label the region $R$.
> 
> > *First draw the three straight lines, *$3x+2y=12$*, *$y=2x$* and *$x=3$
> *You may wish to rearrange *$3x+2y=12$* to the form *$y=mx+c$* first:*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 y & = & - 3 x + 12 \\ y & = & - \frac{3}{2} x + 6\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *The line *$3x+2y\geq12$* takes a solid line because of the "≥"*
> *The lines *$y<2x$* and *$x<3$* take dotted lines because of the "<"*
> 
> ![Graph of lines from question](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/892486116533-ha0m6zse-picture2.png)
> 
> > *Now we need to determine the wanted and unwanted** **regions*
> 
> > *For *$3x+2y\geq12$* (or *$y\geq-\frac{3}{2}x+6$*), the wanted region is above the line*
> *We can check this with the point (0, 0)*
> 
> $3 \left(0\right) + 2 \left(0\right) \geq 12$* is false, so (0, 0) does not lie in the wanted region for *$\begin{aligned}3 x + 2 y & \geq & 12\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *For *$y<2x$*, the wanted region is below the line*
> *If unsure, check with another point, for example (1, 0)*
> 
> $0 < 2 \left(1\right)$* is true, so (1, 0) lies in the wanted region for *$\begin{aligned}y & < & 2 x\end{aligned}$
> 
> *For *$x<3$*, the wanted region is to the left of *$x=3$* *
> *(If unsure, you could check with a point)*
> 
> > *Finally, shade the region that satisfies all three inequalities on the graph*
> *Don't forget to label the region **R*
> 
> ![Graph of region defined by inequalities](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/b98be00422ec-wdtzmk4k-picture3.png)

## Interpreting Graphical Inequalities

> **Spec point** — `3E`

## Interpreting Graphical Inequalities

### How do I determine the inequalities if given a region on a graph?

- **STEP 1**
Write down the **equation** of each line on the graph
- **STEP 2**
Remember that lines are drawn with:

  - A **solid** line for ≤ or ≥ (to indicate line included in region)
  - A **dashed** line for < or > (to indicate line not included)
- **STEP 3**
**Replace** = sign with:

  - ≤ or < if shading **below** line
  - ≥ or > if shading **above** line
  
    - Use a point to test if not sure

### How do I find optimal solutions from a region on an inequalities graph?

- A question may ask you to **optimise** a function for points in the region

  - For example, "For all points in the region with coordinates $\left(x ,  y\right)$,  $P=3x-2y$. Find the greatest value of $P$."
- In these questions the **inequalities** will usually all be ≤ or ≥

  - This means all the points on the lines are **included** in the region
- The **optimal** solution (**minimum** or **maximum**) will always occur at a point where two lines **intersect**

  - **Substitute **the coordinates of the intersection points into the function
  - Choose the point which gives the **maximum** or **minimum** value, as required
  - If the question asks for **integer** solutions
  
    - **Check** that the optimal intersection point coordinates are both integers
    - If they are not, the solution will occur at the point with integer coordinates **nearest** the optimal intersection

> **Worked Example**
> (a)  Write down the three inequalities that define the shaded region in the diagram below.
> 
> ![Graph of region defined by inequalities](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/efd5ee71d965-q14akeze-picture6.png)
> 
> > *Start by determining the equations of the three lines on the graph.*
> 
> > *The line through points (0, 0) and (1, 6) has equation  *$y=6x$
> *The line through points (0, 0) and (2, 2) has equation  *$y=x$
> *The line through points (0, 7) and (7, 0) has equation  *$y=-x+7$
> 
> > *Label the lines on the diagram with these equations*
> 
> ![Graph with equations of lines added on](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/47a98d11c2ac-picture4.png)
> 
> > *The lines are solid, so all the inequalities will be *$\leq$* or *$\geq$
> 
> > *The region is **below** the lines  *$y=-x+7$*  and  *$y=6x$*, so those will be *$\leq$
> *The region is **above** the line  *$y=x$*, so that will be *$\geq$
> 
> > *Write down these inequalities for the final answer*
> 
> $y\leq-x+7,y\leq6x$*  **and***  **$y\geqx$**   **
> 
> For all points in the shaded region, with coordinates $\left(x ,  y\right)$,  $P=20x-3y$.
> 
> (b) Find the greatest value of $P$.
> 
> > *The greatest (and least) values of *$P$* will occur at one of the intersections of the lines bordering the region*
> 
> > *(These points can be seen on the graph, but it would be worth substituting the coordinates into the equations to make sure)*
> 
> > *So we need to find the value of *$P$* at each of those points*
> 
> *For point (0, 0):  *$P = 20 \left(0\right) - 3 \left(0\right) = 0$
> 
> *For point (1, 6):  *$P = 20 \left(1\right) - 3 \left(6\right) = 2$
> 
> *For point (3.5, 3.5):  *$P = 20 \left(3 . 5\right) - 3 \left(3 . 5\right) = 59 . 5$
> 
> **Final answer:** **The greatest value is**** **$P=59.5$

title: Solving Inequalities
bodyMd:
# Solving Inequalities

## Solving Linear Inequalities

> **Spec point** — `3D`

## Solving Linear Inequalities

### What is a linear inequality?

- An **inequality** tells you that one expression is greater than (“>”) or less than (“<”) another

  - “⩾” means “greater than or equal to”
  - “⩽” means “less than or equal to”
- A **linear inequality** only has constant terms (numbers with no letters) and terms in ***x*** (and/or ***y***)

  - but no* ****x***<sup>**2**</sup> terms or terms with other powers of *x*
  
    - 3*x*<sup>2</sup> > 12 is not a linear inequality (it is a **quadratic inequality**)

### How do I solve linear inequalities?

- Solving linear inequalities is just like **solving linear equations**

  - Follow the same rules, but keep the inequality sign throughout
  
    - Changing the inequality sign to an equals sign changes the meaning of the problem
- When you **multiply **or **divide** both sides by a **negative **number, you must **flip the sign** of the inequality

  - e.g. **1 < 2**
  
    - Multiply both sides by –1 (negative number)
    - It becomes **–1 > –2 **(sign flips)
- **Never multiply **or **divide** by a **variable **(*x*)

  - It could be **positive or negative**
- The **safest way **to rearrange is simply to **add & subtract** to move all the terms onto one side
- You also need to know how to

  - use **set notation**
  - deal with **“double” inequalities**

### How do I represent linear inequalities using set notation?

- We use **curly brackets** and a** colon** in **set notation**

  - $\left\{x :  . . .\right\}$ means "*x* is in the set such that ..."
  
    - e.g. the set of all *x *such that *x *is greater than 3 is written $\left\{x :  x > 3\right\}$

- If *x * is **between** two values

  - you can write it as a single set
  
    - e.g. if *x* is greater than 3 **and** less than or equal to 5, then in set notation $\left\{x :  3 < x \leq 5\right\}$
  - or you can write it as separate sets, using the **intersection** symbol, $\cap$
  
    - so the above example could also be written in set notation as $\left\{x : x > 3\right\} \cap \left\{x : x \leq 5\right\}$
  - Either way will get the marks, unless a question specifically **asks for** one or the other

- If *x * is **less than one value OR greater than another value** (disjoint sets)

  - then the two end values must be written in separate sets using the **union** symbol, $\cup$
  
    - e.g. if *x* is less than 3 **or** greater than or equal to 5, then in set notation $\left\{x : x < 3\right\} \cup \left\{x : \geq 5\right\}$

### How do I solve double inequalities?

- Inequalities such as $a<2x<b$ can be solved by doing the same thing to **all three parts** of the inequality

  - Use the same rules as solving linear inequalities

> **Exam Hint**
> - Do not change the inequality sign to an equals when solving linear inequalities
> 
>   - You will lose marks in an exam for doing this.
> - Remember to **reverse the direction** of the inequality sign when **multiplying** or **dividing** by a **negative** number!

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Solve the inequality $-7\leq3x-1<2$.
> 
> > *This is a double inequality, so any operation carried out to one side must be done to all three parts.*
> *Use the expression in the middle to choose the inverse operations needed to isolate **x.*
> 
> > *Add 1 to all three parts.*
> *Remember not to change the inequality signs.*
> 
> $-6\leq3x<3$
> 
> > *Divide all three parts by 3.*
> *3 is positive so there is no need to flip the signs.*
> 
> $-2\leqx<1$
> 
> (b) Write your answer to part (a) in set notation as the intersection of two sets.
> 
> > *Rewrite your answer using the set notation rules discussed above*
> 
> $\left\{x : x \geq - 2\right\} \cap \left\{x : x < 1\right\}$

> **Worked Example**
> Solve the inequality $5-2x\leq21$.
> 
> > *Subtract 5 from both sides, keeping the inequality sign the same*
> 
> $-2x\leq16$
> 
> > *Now divide both sides by -2.*
> *However because you are dividing by a negative number, you must flip the inequality sign*
> 
> $x\geq-8$
> 
> > *The final answer is normally written with the number first, but you won't be penalised for writing the **x** first so long as the inequality sign is the correct way around*
> 
> $x\geq-8$  **or ** $-8\leqx$

## Solving Quadratic Inequalities

> **Spec point** — `3D`

## Solving Quadratic Inequalities

### What are quadratic inequalities?

- A **quadratic inequality **is an inequality with a term in *x*<sup>2</sup> (but no higher powers of *x*)
- Solving the inequality requires solving the corresponding **quadratic equation**
- Sketching a quadratic **graph** is essential

![Solution of a quadratic inequality](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/c6826b8399d3-2-4-2-quadratic-inequalities-notes-diagram-1.png)

### How do I solve quadratic inequalities?

- **STEP 1**
**Rearrange** the inequality into quadratic form with a **positive squared term**

  - ***ax***<sup>**2**</sup>** + *****bx***** + *****c***** > 0**  with  ***a***** > 0**
  
    - The inequality sign may be >, <, ≤ or ≥
- **STEP 2**
Find the **roots** of the quadratic equation

  - **Solve** *ax*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c *= 0 to get ***x***<sub>**1**</sub>* *and* ****x***<sub>**2 **</sub>where** *****x***<sub>**1**</sub>** < *****x***<sub>**2**</sub>
- **STEP 3**
**Sketch** a graph of the quadratic and **label the roots**

  - As the squared term is positive it will be **"U" shaped**
- **STEP 4**
**Identify** the **region** that satisfies the inequality

  - For ***ax***<sup>**2**</sup>** + *****bx***** + *****c***** > 0 **you want the region **above** the *x*-axis
  
    - The solution is ***x *****< *****x***<sub>**1**</sub> **or** ***x *****> *****x***<sub>**2**</sub>** **
    - It is ***x *****≤ *****x***<sub>**1**</sub> **or** ***x *****≥ *****x***<sub>**2**</sub>** **if the original inequality was ≥ instead of >
  - For ***ax***<sup>**2**</sup>** + *****bx***** + *****c***** < 0 **you want the region below the *x*-axis
  
    - The solution is ***x >***** *****x***<sub>**1**</sub> **and** ***x *****< *****x***<sub>**2**</sub>**  **
    - This is more commonly written as ***x***<sub>**1**</sub>** < *****x***** < *****x***<sub>**2**</sub>
    - It is ***x ≥***** *****x***<sub>**1**</sub> **and** ***x ≤***** *****x***<sub>**2**</sub>**  **(***x***<sub>**1**</sub>** *****≤***** *****x***** *****≤***** *****x***<sub>**2**</sub>**) **if the original inequality was ≤ instead of <
- **Avoid** multiplying or dividing by a negative number

  - If unavoidable, remember to “**flip**” the inequality sign (so **<** → **>**, **≥** → **≤**, etc)
- **Avoid** multiplying or dividing by a **variable** (**x**)

  - The variable **could** be negative
  - Multiplying or dividing by ***x***<sup>**2**</sup> is allowed
  
    - However this can create extra invalid solutions
- **Do** rearrange to make the x<sup>2</sup> term positive

![2.4.2 Quadratic Inequalities Notes Diagram 3, Edexcel A Level Maths: Pure revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/a987bc96b9c7-2-4-2-quadratic-inequalities-notes-diagram-3.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - Always start by rearranging to a quadratic with positive squared term
> - Always sketch a graph of the quadratic before deciding the final answer

> **Worked Example**
> ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/5a335e17126e-2-4-2-quadratic-inequalities-example-diagram.png)

title: Completing the Square
bodyMd:
# Completing the Square

## Completing the Square

> **Spec point** — `2A`

## Completing the Square

### How can I rewrite the first two terms of a quadratic expression as the difference of two squares?

- Look at the **quadratic expression** $x^{2}+bx+c$* *
- The first** two terms** can be written as the **difference of two squares** using the following rule

$x^{2}+bx$ is the same as $\left(x + p\right)^{2} - p^{2}$ where $p$ is **half** of $b$

- **Check** this is true by **expanding** the right-hand side

  - Is $x^{2}+2x$ the same as $\left(x + 1\right)^{2} - 1^{2}$?
  
    - Yes: $\left(x + 1\right) \left(x - 1\right) - 1^{2} = x^{2} + 2 x + 1 - 1 = x^{2} + 2 x$
- This works for **negative values of **$b$ too

  - $x^{2}-20x$ can be written as $\left(x - 10\right)^{2} - \left(- 10\right)^{2}$ which is $\left(x - 10\right)^{2} - 100$
  - A negative $b$ **does not change the sign** at the end

### How do I complete the square?

- **Completing the square** is a way to rewrite a quadratic expression in a form containing a squared bracket
- To complete the square on $x^{2}+10x+9$

  - Use the rule above to replace the first two terms, $x^{2}+10x$*, *with $\left(x + 5\right)^{2} - 5^{2}$
  - add 9:  $\left(x + 5\right)^{2} - 5^{2} + 9$
  - **simplify** the **numbers**:  $\left(x + 5\right)^{2} - 25 + 9$
  - answer: $\left(x + 5\right)^{2} - 16$

### How do I complete the square when there is a coefficient in front of the x<sup>2</sup> term?

- You first need to **take **$a$** out** as a factor of the $x^{2}$ and $x$ terms only

  - $a x^{2} + b x + c = a \left[x^{2} + \frac{b}{a} x\right] + c$
  
    - Use **square-shaped** **brackets** here to avoid confusion with round brackets later
  - For example,  $4 x^{2} + 16 x + 5  =  4 \left[x^{2} + 4 x\right] + 5$
- Then complete the square on the bit **inside** the square brackets: $x^{2}+\frac{b}{a}x$

  - This gives $a \left[\left(x + p\right)^{2} - p^{2}\right] + c$
  
    - where *p* is half of $\frac{b}{a}$
  - $4 \left[x^{2} + 4 x\right] + 5  =  4 \left[\left(x + 2\right)^{2} - 4\right] + 5$
- Finally **multiply** this expression by the $a$ outside the square brackets and **add** the $c$

  - $a \left(x + p\right)^{2} - a p^{2} + c$
  - This looks far more complicated than it is in practice!
  
    - Usually you are asked to give your **final answer** in the form  $a \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$
    - Here  $q=-ap^{2}+c$
  - $4 \left[\left(x + 2\right)^{2} - 4\right] + 5  =  4 \left(x + 2\right)^{2} - 16 + 5  =  4 \left(x + 2\right)^{2} - 11$
- For quadratics like $-x^{2}+bx+c$, do the above with $a=-1$

### How do I find the turning point by completing the square?

- Completing the square helps us find the **turning** **point** on a quadratic graph

  - If $y = \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$ then the turning point is at $\left(- p , q\right)$
  
    - Notice the negative sign in the $x$-coordinate
    - This links to **transformations of graphs** (translating $y=x^{2}$ by $p$ to the left and $q$* *up)
  - If $y = a \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$ then the turning point is still at $\left(- p , q\right)$
  
    - It's a **minimum** point if  $a>0$
    - It's a **maximum** point if  $a<0$
- It can also help you **create the equation** of a quadratic when given the turning point

![Completing the square Notes Diagram 3, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/ef75f3f06e8d-2-2-3-completing-the-square-notes-diagram-3.png)

- It can also be used to **prove** and/or **show** results using the fact that any "squared term", i.e. the bracket (*x* ± *p*)<sup>2</sup> , will always be **greater than or equal to 0**

  - You cannot square a number and get a negative value

![Completing the square Notes Diagram 4, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/a5396a6f9112-2-2-3-completing-the-square-notes-diagram-4.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - Expand your answer to check that you have completed the square correctly.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) By completing the square, find the coordinates of the turning point on the graph of $y=x^{2}+6x-11$.
> 
> > *Find half of *$+6$* (call this *$p$*)*
> * *
> 
> > $p=\frac{6}{2}=3$
> * *
> 
> > *Write *$x^{2}+6x$* in the form *$\left(x + p\right)^{2} - p^{2}$* *
> * *
> 
> $x^{2}+6x$* is the same as *$\left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 3^{2}$
> * *
> 
> > *Put this result into the equation of the curve*
> * *
> 
> > $y = \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 3^{2} - 11$
> * *
> 
> > *Simplify the numbers*
> * *
> 
> > $y = \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 20$
> * *
> 
> > *Use the fact that the turning point of *$y = \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$* is at *$\left(- p , q\right)$
> 
> > *Here *$p=3$* and *$q=-20$
> 
> **Final answer:** **Turning point at **$(-3,-20)$
> 
> (b) Write $-3x^{2}+12x+24$ in the form $a \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$
> 
> > *Factorise *$-3$* out of the first two terms only*
> *Use square-shaped brackets*
> * *
> 
> > $- 3 \left[x^{2} - 4 x\right] + 24$
> * *
> 
> > *Complete the square on the *$x^{2}-4x$* inside the brackets (write in the form *$\left(x + p\right)^{2} - p^{2}$* where *$p$* is half of *$-4$*)*
> * *
> 
> > $- 3 \left[\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - \left(- 2\right)^{2}\right] + 24$
> * *
> 
> > *Simplify the numbers inside the brackets*
> $\left(- 2\right)^{2}$* is *$4$
> * *
> 
> > $- 3 \left[\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 4\right] + 24$
> * *
> 
> > *Multiply all the terms inside the square-shaped brackets by *$-3$
> * *
> 
> > $- 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 12 + 24$
> * *
> 
> > *Simplify the numbers*
> * *
> 
> > $- 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 36$
> * *
> 
> > *This is now in the form *$a \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$* where *$a=-3$*, *$p=-2$* and *$q=36$
> 
> $-3(x-2)^{2}+36$

title: Factorising Quadratics
bodyMd:
# Factorising Quadratics

## Factorising Quadratics

> **Spec point** — `2A`

## Factorising Quadratics

### How can I factorise simple quadratics?

- If there is **no constant term** then just factorise out (a multiple of) $x$

  - $x^{2} - 9 x = x \left(x - 9\right)$
  - $5 x^{2} + 30 x = 5 x \left(x + 6\right)$
- Factorise quadratics of the form $x^{2}+bx+c$ by **inspection**

  - Find a pair of numbers, $p$ and $q$, that **multiply** to give $c$ and **add** to give $b$
  
    - E.g. for $x^{2}-21x-100$ the numbers would be $4$ and $-25$
  - The quadratic will factorise as $\left(x + p\right) \left(x + q\right)$
  
    - So  $x^{2} - 21 x - 100 = \left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 25\right)$

### How can I factorise harder quadratics?

- A **harder quadratic** is of the form $ax^{2}+bx+c$ where $a$ is not equal to 1 (or 0)

  - E.g. $12x^{2}-11x-5$
- These can also be factorised **by inspection**

  - This requires a lot of practice and there are no simple rules to follow
- They can be factorised reliably by **grouping**

  - Find a pair of numbers that **multiply** to $ac$ and **add** to $b$
  
    - For $12x^{2}-11x-5$,  $ac=-60$ and $b=-11$
    - So the two numbers are $4$ and $-15$
  - **Rewrite** the middle $bx$ term using those two numbers
  
    - $12x^{2}+4x-15x-5$
  - **Group** and **factorise** the first two terms and the last two terms by pulling out **common factors**
  
    - $4 x \left(3 x + 1\right) - 5 \left(3 x + 1\right)$
  - Those two terms now have a **common factor** (in brackets) that can be factorised out
  
    - $\left(4 x - 5\right) \left(3 x + 1\right)$

### How do I factorise a difference of two squares

- A **difference** **of two squares **refers to any expression of the form $a^{2}-b^{2}$

  - I.e. 'something squared subtracted from something else squared'
  - For example,
  
    - $x^{2}-36$
    - $9^{2}-5^{2}$
    - $\left(x + 1\right)^{2} - \left(x - 4\right)^{2}$
    - $4m^{2}-25n^{2}$  which is equal to  $\left(2 m\right)^{2} - \left(5 n\right)^{2}$
- Such expressions will **factorise** as $\left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right)$

  - This is because  $\left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right) = a^{2} - a b + a b - b^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}$
  - So
  
    - $x^{2} - 36 = \left(x + 6\right) \left(x - 6\right)$
    - $9^{2} - 5^{2} = \left(9 + 5\right) \left(9 - 5\right)$  which is equal to $14\times4=56$
    - $\left(x + 1\right)^{2} - \left(x - 4\right)^{2} = \left(\left(x + 1\right) + \left(x - 4\right)\right) \left(\left(x + 1\right) - \left(x - 4\right)\right)$ which is equal to $\left(2 x - 3\right) \left(5\right) = 10 x - 15$
    - $4 m^{2} - 25 n^{2} = \left(2 m + 5 n\right) \left(2 m - 5 n\right)$

> **Exam Hint**
> - As a check, expand your answer and make sure you get the same expression as the one you were trying to factorise.
> - You should be able to recognise a difference of squares in both factorised and unfactorised form

> **Worked Example**
> (a)  Factorise $x^{2}-4x-21$.
> 
> > *           We will factorise by inspection*
> 
> > *          We need two numbers that multiply to *$-21$* and add to *$-4$
> 
> > *         *$+3$* and *$-7$* satisfy this*
> 
> > *          Write down the brackets*
> 
> $(x+3)(x-7)$
> 
> (b) Factorise $6x^{2}-7x-3$.
> 
> > *        We will factorise by splitting the middle term and grouping*
> 
> > *        We need two numbers that multiply to  *$6 \times \left(- 3\right) = - 18$*and add to*$-7$* *
> 
> > $+2$*  and *$-9$* satisfy this*
> 
> > *        Split the middle term*
> 
> $6x^{2}+2x-9x-3$
> 
> > *        Factorise *$2x$* out of the first two terms, and *$-3$* out of the last two terms*
> 
> $2 x \left(3 x + 1\right) - 3 \left(3 x + 1\right)$
> 
> > *        These have a common factor of *$\left(3 x + 1\right)$* which can be factored out*
> 
> $(2x-3)(3x+1)$
> 
> (c) Factorise $9x^{2}-16$.
> 
> *Recognise that this is a difference of two squares, because  * * *$9 x^{2} - 16 = \left(3 x\right)^{2} - \left(4\right)^{2}$
> 
> > *         Use the relation  *$a^{2} - b^{2} = \left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right)$
> 
> $(3x+4)(3x-4)$

title: Roots of Quadratic Equations
bodyMd:
# Roots of Quadratic Equations

## Discriminants

> **Spec point** — `2B`

## Discriminants

### What is the discriminant of a quadratic function?

- The **discriminant** of a quadratic is often denoted by the Greek letter $Δ$ (upper case delta)
- For a quadratic  $a x^{2} + b x + c \text{   } \left(a \neq 0\right)$ the discriminant is given by

  - $Δ=b^{2}-4ac$
- The discriminant is the expression that is **inside the square root** in the **quadratic formula**

  - $x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$
- This is not on the exam formula sheet so you need to** remember **it

### How does the discriminant of a quadratic function affect its graph and roots?

- The discriminant tells us about the **roots** (or **solutions**) of the equation  $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$

  - It also tells us about the **graph** of  $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$
- If Δ > 0 then $\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}$ and $-\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}$ are **two distinct values**

  - The equation $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ has **unequal real roots**
  
    - i.e. there are two **distinct real solutions**
  - The graph of $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$ **crosses** the *x*-axis **twice**
- If $Δ=0$ then $\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}$ and $-\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}$ are **both zero**

  - The equation $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ has **equal real roots**
  
    - i.e. it has one **repeated real solution**
  - The** **graph of $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$ **touches** the *x*-axis at **exactly one point**
  
    - This means that the ***x*****-axis** is a **tangent** to the graph
- If $Δ<0$ then $\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}$ and $-\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}$ are **both undefined**

  - The **roots **of the equation $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ are **not real**
  
    - i.e. it has **no real solutions**
  - The** **graph of $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$ **never touches **the** *****x*****-axis**
  
    - This means that graph is **wholly above **(or **below**) the ***x*****-axis**

![Discrimamts Notes Diagram 2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/74e5af0fc89b-2-2-2-discrimamts-notes-diagram-2.png)

### How do I solve problems using the discriminant?

- Often at least one of the coefficients of a quadratic will be given as an **unknown**

  - For example the letter $k$* *may be used* *for the unknown constant
- You will be given a fact about the quadratic such as:

  - The **number of real solutions** of the equation
  - The **number of roots** (i.e. ***x*****-intercepts)** of the graph
- To find the **value or range of values** of $k$

  - Find an **expression for the discriminant**
  
    - Use $Δ=b^{2}-4ac$
  - Decide whether $Δ>0$, $Δ=0$ or $Δ<0$
  
    - If the question says there are **real roots** but does not specify how many then use $Δ\geq0$
  - **Solve** the resulting equation or inequality for $k$

> **Exam Hint**
> - Questions won't always use the word discriminant
> 
>   - It is important to recognise when its use is required
>   - Look for
>   
>     - a number of roots or solutions being stated
>     - whether and/or how often the graph of a quadratic function intercepts the $x$-axis

> **Worked Example**
> A function is given by $f(x)=2kx^{2}+kx-k+2$ , where $k$ is a constant. The graph of $y=f(x)$ intercepts the $x$-axis at two different points.
> 
> a) Show that $9k^{2}-16k>0$.
> 
> > *The question says the graph 'intercepts the **x**-axis at two different points'*
> 
> > *This means that the discriminant *$b^{2}-4ac$* is greater than zero*
> 
> > *Here  *$a=2k$*,  *$b=k$*,  and  *$c=-k+2$
> 
> $\left(k\right)^{2} - 4 \left(2 k\right) \left(- k + 2\right) > 0$
> 
> > *Expand the brackets and collect terms*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}k^{2} - 8 k \left(- k + 2\right) & > & 0 \\ k^{2} + 8 k^{2} - 16 k & > & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> $9k^{2}-16k>0$
> 
> b) Hence find the range of possible values of $k$.
> 
> > *Solve the inequality, beginning by factorising*
> 
> $k \left(9 k - 16\right) > 0$
> 
> > *This tells us the graph of  *$y=9k^{2}-16k$*  intercepts the horizontal axis at *$k=0$* and *$k=\frac{16}{9}$
> 
> > *It can be helpful to sketch a graph here*
> 
> ![Graph for solving quadratic inequality](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/e9e918282f3d-sy-mefmv-picture1.png)
> 
> > $9k^{2}-16k>0$* will be true to the left of 0 and to the right of *$\frac{16}{9}$
> 
> > *Write these down as inequalities*
> 
> $k<0\mathrm{or}k>\frac{16}{9}$

## Sum & Product of Roots

> **Spec point** — `2C`

## Sum & Product of Roots

### How are the roots of a quadratic equation linked to its coefficients?

- A **quadratic equation** $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ (where $a\neq0$) has **roots** $α$ and $β$ given by

  - $α,β=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$
  
    - i.e. the **solutions** found by the **quadratic formula** (or any other solution method)
- This means the equation can be **rewritten** in the form  $a(x-α)(x-β)=0$

  - Note that $(x-α)(x-β)=x^{2}-(α+β)x+αβ$
  
    - It is possible that the roots are repeated, i.e. that $α=β$
  - You can then **equate** the two forms:
  
    - $ax^{2}+bx+c=a(x-α)(x-β)$
  - Then (because $a\neq0$) you can **divide** both sides of that by *a* and **expand** the brackets:
  
    - $x^{2}+\frac{b}{a}x+\frac{c}{a}=x^{2}-(α+β)x+αβ$
  - Finally, **compare the coefficients**
  
    - $x$ coefficients:  $-\frac{b}{a}=(α+β)$
    - Constant terms:  $\frac{c}{a}=αβ$

- Therefore for a quadratic equation $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$  :

  - The **sum of the roots** $α+β$ is equal to $-\frac{b}{a}$
  - The **product of the roots** $αβ$ is equal to $\frac{c}{a}$
- You **don't** need to **prove** these results on the exam

  - But you need to be able to **use** them to answer questions about quadratics
  - They are **not** on the exam **formula sheet**
  
    - So you need to **remember** (or be able to **derive**) them
- You can use them

  - to **find the** **sum** **and product of the roots** if you know the equation
  
    - Just substitute $a$, $b$ and $c$ into the formulae
  - or to **find the equation** if you know the sum and product of the roots
  
    - See the next section

### How do I find a quadratic equation from information about its roots?

- You may be **given** the **sum** and **product** of an equation's roots and then asked to **find the equation**

  - Usually the equation will need to have **integer coefficients**
  
    - For example  "A quadratic equation has roots $α$ and $β$, where  $α+β=\frac{7}{2}$  and  $αβ=-2$. Find a quadratic equation with integer coefficients that has roots $α$ and $β$."
- **STEP 1**
Start with the **formulae** linking the roots and coefficients

  - $α+β=-\frac{b}{a}$
  
    - So  $\frac{b}{a}=-\frac{7}{2}$
  - $αβ=\frac{c}{a}$
  
    - So  $\frac{c}{a}=-2$
- **STEP 2**
**Choose** a value for $a$, and find the **corresponding values** for $b$ and $c$

  - Choose a value for $a$ that will **multiply** to make the values for $α+β$ and $αβ$ into **integers**
  
    - Let $a=2$
    - Then  $b=-\frac{7}{2}\times2=-7$
    - And  $c=-2\times2=-4$
- **STEP 3**
**Write down** the equation using your values for $a$, $b$ and $c$

  - $2x^{2}-7x-4=0$
- Note that the answer is **not unique**

  - Any** multiple **of the equation will also have the **same roots**
  
    - e.g.  $4x^{2}-14x-8=0$

### How do I find a quadratic equation with related roots?

- You may be asked to find a quadratic equation whose roots are **related to the roots** of another quadratic equation

  - I.e. whose roots are expressed in terms of the roots of the first equation
- You will often need **algebraic tricks** to write other expressions with $α$ and $β$ **in terms of** $α+β$ and $αβ$

  - $α$ and $β$ are the roots of the first quadratic
  - For example:
  
    - $\begin{aligned}\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} & = & \alpha^{2} + 2 \alpha \beta + \beta^{2} - 2 \alpha \beta \\ & = & \left(\alpha + \beta\right)^{2} - 2 \alpha \beta\end{aligned}$
    - $\begin{aligned}\alpha^{3} + \beta^{3} & = & \alpha^{3} + 3 \alpha \beta \left(\alpha + \beta\right) + \beta^{3} - 3 \alpha \beta \left(\alpha + \beta\right) \\ & = & \alpha^{3} + 3 \alpha^{2} \beta + 3 \alpha \beta^{2} + \beta^{3} - 3 \alpha \beta \left(\alpha + \beta\right) \\ & = & \left(\alpha + \beta\right)^{3} - 3 \alpha \beta \left(\alpha + \beta\right)\end{aligned}$
    - $\begin{aligned}\left(\alpha - \beta\right)^{2} & = & \alpha^{2} - 2 \alpha \beta + \beta^{2} \\ & = & \alpha^{2} + 2 \alpha \beta + \beta^{2} - 4 \alpha \beta \\ & = & \left(\alpha + \beta\right)^{2} - 4 \alpha \beta\end{aligned}$

- Then if you know the values of $α+β$ and $αβ$ from the **first quadratic**, you can use them to find the **sum** or **product** of the **new roots**

  - For example "A quadratic equation has roots $α$ and $β$ where  $α+β=-\frac{3}{2}$  and  $αβ=2$.  Form a second quadratic equation with integer coefficients that has roots $\frac{α}{β^{2}}$ and $\frac{β}{α^{2}}$."
  - The **sum** of the new roots is  $\frac{\alpha}{\beta^{2}} + \frac{\beta}{\alpha^{2}} = \frac{\alpha^{3} + \beta^{3}}{\alpha^{2} \beta^{2}} = \frac{\alpha^{3} + \beta^{3}}{\left(\alpha \beta\right)^{2}}$
  
    - We can use the substitution for $α^{3}+β^{3}$ from above
    - So  $Sum = \frac{\left(\alpha + \beta\right)^{3} - 3 \alpha \beta \left(\alpha + \beta\right)}{\left(\alpha \beta\right)^{2}} = \frac{\left(- \frac{3}{2}\right)^{3} - 3 \left(2\right) \left(- \frac{3}{2}\right)}{\left(2\right)^{2}} = \frac{45}{32}$
  - The **product** of the new roots is  $\frac{α}{β^{2}}\times\frac{β}{α^{2}}=\frac{αβ}{α^{2}β^{2}}=\frac{1}{αβ}$
  
    - So  $\mathrm{Product}=\frac{1}{αβ}=\frac{1}{2}$
  - With the sum and product we can **form the equation** as described in the last section
  
    - $32x^{2}-45x+16=0$

> **Worked Example**
> The roots of the quadratic equation $2x^{2}-11x+5=0$ are $α$ and $β$.
> 
> Given that  $α>β$  and without solving the equation,
> 
> (a)  show that  $α-β=\frac{9}{2}$
> 
> > *Use  *$α+β=-\frac{b}{a}$*  and *$αβ=\frac{c}{a}$*  to find the sum and product*
> 
> $\alpha + \beta = - \frac{\left(- 11\right)}{2} = \frac{11}{2}$
> 
> $αβ=\frac{5}{2}$
> 
> > *Express *$\left(\alpha - \beta\right)^{2}$* in terms of  *$α+β$*  and  *$αβ$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}\left(\alpha - \beta\right)^{2} & = & \alpha^{2} - 2 \alpha \beta + \beta^{2} \\ & = & \left(\alpha^{2} + 2 \alpha \beta + \beta^{2}\right) - 4 \alpha \beta \\ & = & \left(\alpha + \beta\right)^{2} - 4 \alpha \beta\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Substitute to find the value*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}\left(\alpha - \beta\right)^{2} & = & \left(\frac{11}{2}\right)^{2} - 4 \left(\frac{5}{2}\right) \\ & = & \frac{121}{4} - 10 \\ & = & \frac{81}{4}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Take the square root, remembering the *$\pm$
> 
> $α-β=\pm\frac{9}{2}$
> 
> > *Finally, use the fact that *$α>β$
> 
> *But  *$α>β$*,  therefore  *$α-β>0$
> 
> $α-β=\frac{9}{2}$
> 
> (b) form a quadratic equation, with integer coefficients, which has roots  $\frac{α+β}{α}$ and $\frac{α-β}{β}$
> 
> > *Start by finding the sum and product of the new roots*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}Sum & = & \frac{\alpha + \beta}{a} + \frac{\alpha - \beta}{\beta} \\ & = & \frac{\beta \left(\alpha + \beta\right) + \alpha \left(\alpha - \beta\right)}{\alpha \beta} \\ & = & \frac{\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2}}{\alpha \beta} \\ & = & \frac{\left(\alpha^{2} + 2 \alpha \beta + \beta^{2}\right) - 2 \alpha \beta}{\alpha \beta} \\ & = & \frac{\left(\alpha + \beta\right)^{2} - 2 \alpha \beta}{\alpha \beta} \\ & = & \frac{\left(\frac{11}{2}\right)^{2} - 2 \left(\frac{5}{2}\right)}{\frac{5}{2}} \\ & = & \frac{101}{10} \\ & & \\ & & \\ Product & = & \frac{\alpha + \beta}{a} \times \frac{\alpha - \beta}{\beta} \\ & = & \frac{\left(\alpha + \beta\right) \left(\alpha - \beta\right)}{\alpha \beta} \\ & = & \frac{\left(\frac{11}{2}\right) \left(\frac{9}{2}\right)}{\frac{5}{2}} \\ & = & \frac{99}{10}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Now use  *$\mathrm{Sum} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{roots}=-\frac{b}{a}$*  and  *$\mathrm{Product} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{roots}=\frac{c}{a}$
> 
> $\frac{b}{a}=-\frac{101}{10}\mathrm{and}\frac{c}{a}=\frac{99}{10}$
> 
> > *Select  *$a=10$*  so *$b$* and *$c$* will have integer values*
> 
> $a=10b=-101c=99$
> 
> > *And finally use those coefficients to write the new equation*
> 
> $10x^{2}-101x+99=0$

title: Solving Quadratic Equations
bodyMd:
# Solving Quadratic Equations

## Solving Quadratic Equations

> **Spec point** — `2B`

## Solving Quadratic Equations

You should be familiar with solving quadratic equations from your IGCSE Mathematics course.
This is a quick revision guide about the different methods and when to use them.**  **

### When should I solve by factorisation?

- When the question asks to** solve by factorisation**

  - For example, part (a) Factorise $6x^{2}+7x-3$, part (b) Solve $6x^{2}+7x-3=0$
  
    - Factorises as  $\left(3 x - 1\right) \left(2 x + 3\right) = 0$
    - Solutions are  $x=\frac{1}{3}$  and  $x=-\frac{3}{2}$
- When solving **two-term quadratic equations**

  - For example, solve $x^{2}-4x=0$
  
    - Take out a **common factor **of $x$ to get $x \left(x - 4\right) = 0$
    - Solutions are $x=0$ and $x=4$
  - For example, solve $x^{2}-9=0$
  
    - Use **difference of two squares** to factorise it as $\left(x + 3\right) \left(x - 3\right) = 0$
    - Solutions are $x=-3$ and $x=3$
    - (Could also rearrange to $x^{2}=9$ and use ±√ to get $x=\pm3$)

### When should I use the quadratic formula?

- When the question says to leave solutions correct to** **a** given accuracy** (2 decimal places, 3 significant figures etc)
- When the quadratic formula may be **faster** than factorising

  - It's quicker to solve $36x^{2}+33x-20=0$ using the quadratic formula than by factorisation
- **If in doubt**, use the quadratic formula - it always works
- You must **remember** the formula however - it isn't on the exam formula sheet
- If  $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$,  the **solutions** are

  - $x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$

### When should I solve by completing the square?

- When part (a) of a question says to **complete the square** and part (b) says to use part (a) to solve the equation
- When making $x$ the **subject of harder formulae** containing $x^{2}$ and $x$ terms

  - For example, make $x$ the subject of the formula  $x^{2}+6x=y$
  
    - Complete the square: $\left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 9 = y$
    - Add 9 to both sides: $\left(x + 3\right)^{2} = y + 9$
    - Take square roots and use ±:  $x+3=\pm\sqrt{y+9}$
    - Subtract 3:  $x=-3\pm\sqrt{y+9}$
- Like the quadratic formula, completing the square will **always work**

  - But it is not always quick or easy to use the method

> **Exam Hint**
> - Some calculators can solve quadratic equations
> 
>   - Even if you need to show working you can use a calculator to check your solutions
>   - If the calculator solutions are whole numbers or fractions (with no square roots), this means the quadratic can be factorised

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Solve $x^{2}-7x+2=0$, giving your answers correct to 2 decimal places
> 
> > *“Correct to 2 decimal places” suggests using the quadratic formula*
> *Substitute *$a=1$*, *$b=-7$* and *$c=2$* into the formula, putting brackets around any negative numbers*
> * *
> 
> $x = \frac{- \left(- 7\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(- 7\right)^{2} - 4 \times 1 \times 2}}{2 \times 1}$
> 
> > *Use a calculator to find each solution *
> 
> $x=6.7015...\mathrm{or}x=0.2984...$* *
> 
> > *Round your final answers to 2 decimal places*
> 
> $x=6.70\mathrm{or}x=0.30$  **(2 d.p.)**
> 
> (b) Solve $16x^{2}-82x+45=0$
> 
> > *Method 1*
> *If you cannot spot the factorisation, use the quadratic formula*
> *Substitute** *$a=16$*, *$b=-82$* and *$c=45$* into the formula, putting brackets around any negative numbers*
> 
> $x = \frac{- \left(- 82\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(- 82\right)^{2} - 4 \times 16 \times 45}}{2 \times 16}$
> 
> > *Use a calculator to find each solution*
> 
> **Final answer:** $x=\frac{9}{2}$**  or **$x=\frac{5}{8}$
> 
> > *Method 2*
> *If you do spot the factorisation, (2x – 9)(8x – 5), then use that method instead *
> 
> > $\left(2 x - 9\right) \left(8 x - 5\right) = 0$* *
> 
> > *Set the first bracket equal to zero *
> 
> > $2x-9=0$* *
> 
> > *Add 9 to both sides then divide by 2 *
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 x & = & 9 \\ x & = & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Set the second bracket equal to zero *
> 
> > $8x-5=0$* *
> 
> > *Add 5 to both sides then divide by 8 *
> 
> $\begin{aligned}8 x & = & 5 \\ x & = & \frac{5}{8}\end{aligned}$
> 
> $x=\frac{9}{2}\mathrm{or}x=\frac{5}{8}$
> 
> ** **(c) By writing $x^{2}+6x+5$ in the form $\left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$, solve $x^{2}+6x+5=0$
> 
> > *This question wants you to complete the square first*
> *Find *$p$* (by halving the middle number) *
> 
> > $p=\frac{6}{2}=3$* *
> 
> > *Write *$x^{2}+6x$* as *$\left(x + p\right)^{2} - p^{2}$
> <sup>* *</sup>
> 
> $\begin{aligned}x^{2} + 6 x & = & \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 3^{2} \\ & = & \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 9\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Replace *$x^{2}+6x$* **with *$\left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 9$* in the equation *
> 
> $\begin{aligned}\left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 9 + 5 & = & 0 \\ \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 4 & = & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Make *$x$* the subject of the equation*
> *Start by adding 4 to both sides *
> 
> > $\left(x + 3\right)^{2} = 4$* *
> 
> > *Take square roots of both sides (include a ± sign to get both solutions) *
> 
> > $x+3=\pm\sqrt{4}=\pm2$* *
> 
> > *Subtract 3 from both sides *
> 
> > $x=-3\pm2$* *
> 
> > *Find each solution separately using + first, then - second*
> 
> $x=-5\mathrm{or}x=-1$
> 
> **Even though the quadratic factorises to **$\left(x + 5\right) \left(x + 1\right)$**, this is not the method asked for in the question**

title: Arcs & Sectors
bodyMd:
# Arcs & Sectors

## Length of an Arc

> **Spec point** — `10A`

## Length of an Arc

### What is an arc?

- An arc is a part of the **circumference **of a circle

  - You can think of it as the crust on a slice of pizza
- The **length** of an arc depends on

  - the size of the **angle at the centre** of the circle
  - the **radius** of the circle
- If the angle at the centre is **less than 180°** then the arc is known as a **minor arc**
- If the angle at the centre is **more than 180°** then the arc is known as a **major arc**

### How do I find the length of an arc using degrees?

- The **length** **of an arc** is simply a **fraction** of the total circumference of a circle

  - The fraction can be **found** by dividing the angle at the centre by 360°
- The **formula** for the length, $l$, of an arc is

  - $l=\frac{θ}{360}\times2πr$

- $θ$ is the **angle** measured in **degrees**
- $r$ is the **radius**
- This is **not** on the exam formula sheet, so you need to remember it

### How do I find the length of an arc using radians?

- When working in **radians** the formula for arc length is much simpler

  - This is because $π$ is already 'built into' radians
- The **formula** for the length, $l$, of an arc is

  - $l=rθ$

- $θ$ is the **angle** measured in **radians**
- $r$ is the **radius**
- This is **not** on the exam formula sheet, so you need to remember it

> **Exam Hint**
> - Be careful on arc length questions
> 
>   - Finding the arc length may only be part of a larger question
>   - For example finding the total perimeter of a circle sector
> - Make sure you are using the formula that matches the angle measure (degrees or radians)

> **Worked Example**
> A circular pizza has had a slice cut from it. The slice is in the shape of a sector, with the angle at the centre being 38°. The radius of the pizza is 12 cm.
> 
> (a) Find the length of the outside crust of the slice of pizza (the minor arc), giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
> 
> > *Drawing a diagram can help with questions like this*
> 
> ![Minor sector with minor arc, angle and radius](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/f508908880f1-igcse-fpure-arc-length-we-1.png)
> 
> > *Use the arc length formula (in the degrees form) with *$r=12$* and *$θ=38$
> *(You could also convert *$38^{\circ}$* to radians and use the radians version of the formula)*
> 
> $l = \frac{38}{360} \times 2 \pi \left(12\right) = \frac{38 \pi}{15} = 7 . 958701 . . .$
> 
> > *Round to 3 significant figures*
> 
> > *(Note that *$\frac{38π}{15}$* cm is the exact value answer)*
> 
> $7.96\mathrm{cm}(3s.f.)$
> 
> (b) Find the perimeter of the remaining pizza, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
> 
> > *Drawing a diagram can help*
> 
> > *The remaining pizza will be in the shape of a major sector*
> 
> > *The angle at the centre will be  *$360-38=322^{\circ}$
> 
> ![Major sector of circle with radius and angle at centre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/040aa54c3c7e-igcse-fpure-arc-length-we-2.png)
> 
> > *The perimeter will include both the major arc and the two radii*
> 
> > *Use the arc length formula (in the degrees form) with *$r=12$* and *$θ=322$
> 
> $perimeter = \left(\frac{322}{360} \times 2 \pi \left(12\right)\right) + 12 + 12 = \frac{322 \pi}{15} + 24 = 91 . 439522 . . .$
> 
> > *Round to 3 significant figures*
> 
> > *(Note that *$\frac{322π}{15}+24$* cm is the exact value answer)*
> 
> **Final answer:** **91.4 cm (3 s.f.)**

> **Worked Example**
> A sector of a circle has a radius of 7cm and an angle at the centre of $\frac{π}{6}$ radians. Find the perimeter of the sector, giving your answer as an exact value.
> 
> > *Drawing a diagram can help*
> 
> ![Circle sector with radius and angle at centre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/eee72845cbd2-igcse-fpure-arc-length-we-3.png)
> 
> > *The perimeter of sector will include both the length of the arc and the two radii*
> 
> > *Use the arc length formula (in the radians form) with *$r=7$* and *$θ=\frac{π}{6}$
> 
> $perimeter = \left(7\right) \left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) + 7 + 7 = \frac{7 \pi}{6} + 14$
> 
> > *The question asks for an exact value answer, so just write that down (with units!)*
> 
> $\frac{7π}{6}+14\mathrm{cm}$

## Area of a Sector

> **Spec point** — `10A`

## Area of a Sector

### What is a sector?

- A **sector** is a part of a circle enclosed by **two radii** (radiuses) and an **arc**

  - You can think of this as the shape of a single slice of pizza
- The **area** of a sector depends on

  - the size of the angle at the centre of the sector
  - the **radius** of the circle
- If the angle at the centre is **less than 180°** then the sector is known as a **minor sector**
- If the angle at the centre is **more than 180°** then the sector is known as a **major sector**

### How do I find the area of a sector using degrees?

- The **area of a sector** is simply a **fraction** of the area of the whole circle

  - The fraction can be found by dividing the angle at the centre by 360°
- The **formula** for the area, $A$, of a sector is

  - $A=\frac{θ}{360}\timesπr^{2}$

- $θ$ is the **angle** measured in degrees
- $r$ is the **radius**
- This is **not** on the formula sheet, so you need to remember it

### How do I find the area of a sector using radians?

- When working in **radians** the formula for sector area is much simpler

  - This is because $π$ is already 'built into' radians
- The **formula** for the area, $A$, of a sector is

  - $A=\frac{1}{2}r^{2}θ$

- $θ$ is the **angle** measured in radians
- $r$ is the **radius**
- This is **not** on the formula sheet, so you need to remember it

> **Exam Hint**
> - Make sure you are using the formula that matches the angle measure (degrees or radians)

> **Worked Example**
> Jamie has divided a circle of radius 50 cm into two sectors: a minor sector of angle 100°, and a major sector of angle 260°. He is going to paint the minor sector blue and the major sector yellow.
> 
> (a) Find the area Jamie will paint blue, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures
> 
> > *Drawing a diagram can be helpful in questions like this*
> 
> ![Circle with minor and major sectors](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/1aa0e8a333da-igcse-fpure-sector-area-we-1.png)
> 
> > *Use the sector area formula (degrees form) with *$r=50$* and *$θ=100$
> 
> > *(You could also convert *$100^{\circ}$* to radians and use the radians version of the formula)*
> 
> $A = \frac{100}{360} \times \pi \left(50\right)^{2} = \frac{6250 \pi}{9} = 2181 . 6615 . . .$
> 
> > *Round to 3 significant figures*
> 
> > *(Note that *$\frac{6250π}{9}$* cm*<sup>*2*</sup>* is the exact value answer) *
> 
> $2180\mathrm{cm}^{2}(3s.f.)$
> 
> (b) Find the area Jamie will paint yellow, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
> 
> > *This will be the rest of the circle from the preceding diagram*
> 
> > *Use the sector area formula (degrees form) with *$r=50$* and *$θ=260$
> 
> $A = \frac{260}{160} \times \pi \left(50\right)^{2} = \frac{16250 \pi}{9} = 5672 . 3200 . . .$
> 
> > *Round to 3 significant figures*
> 
> > *(Note that *$\frac{16250π}{9}$* cm*<sup>*2*</sup>* is the exact value answer)*
> 
> $5670\mathrm{cm}^{2}(3s.f.)$

> **Worked Example**
> A sector of a circle has a radius of 7 cm and an angle at the centre of $\frac{π}{6}$ radians. Find the area of the sector, giving your answer as an exact value.
> 
> > *Drawing a diagram can help*
> 
> ![Circle sector with radius and angle a centre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/eee72845cbd2-igcse-fpure-arc-length-we-3.png)
> 
> > *Use the sector area formula (radians form) with *$r=7$* and *$θ=\frac{π}{6}$
> 
> $A = \frac{1}{2} \left(7\right)^{2} \left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{49 \pi}{12}$
> 
> > *The question asks for an exact value answer, so just write that down (with units!)*
> 
> $\frac{49π}{12}\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

title: Radian Measure
bodyMd:
# Radian Measure

## Radian Measure

> **Spec point** — `10A`

## Radian Measure

### What are radians?

- **Radians** are an alternative to degrees for measuring angles
- 1 radian is **defined** as the angle in a circle **sector** of radius 1 and arc length 1
- Radians are often given in terms of $π$

  - $2π$ radians = 360°
  - $π$ radians = 180°
- The **symbol** for radians is <sup>c</sup> but it is more usual to see **rad**

  - When $π$ is involved, **no symbol** for radians is needed
  
    - With $π$ it is obvious it is in radians
  - You should **never** omit the symbol for degrees
- In the exam a question will usually tell you **which angle measure** to use

  - But radians **must** be used if calculus with the trigonometric functions is involved

![1 radian shown on a unit circle](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/7b5234c20288-5-4-1-radian-measure-notes-diagram-1.png)

### How do I convert between radians and degrees?

- Use $π$* *radians<sup> </sup>= 180° to **convert** between radians and degrees

  - To convert **from radians to degrees** multiply by $\frac{180}{π}$
  - To convert **from degrees to radians** multiply by $\frac{π}{180}$
- Some of the **common equivalents** are:

  - $2π\mathrm{rad}=360^{\circ}$
  - $π\mathrm{rad}=180^{\circ}$
  - $\frac{π}{2}\mathrm{rad}=90^{\circ}$
  - $\frac{π}{3}\mathrm{rad}=60^{\circ}$
  - $\frac{π}{4}\mathrm{rad}=45^{\circ}$
  - $\frac{π}{6}\mathrm{rad}=30^{\circ}$
- It is useful to **remember** these and use them to work out other conversions
- Your **calculator** will be able to work with both radians and degrees

![using multiples or fractions of pi when converting between radians and degrees](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/bb6a9c0e8fdb-5-4-1-radian-measure-notes-diagram-2.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> - If the question specifies a unit of angle measure (radians or degrees) be sure to use it!
> - Make sure that your calculator is in the correct mode for the angle measure you are working with

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Convert 43.8° to radians, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
> 
> > *Multiply by  *$\frac{π}{180}$
> 
> $43.8\times\frac{π}{180}=\frac{73π}{300}=0.764454...$
> 
> > *Note that *$\frac{73π}{300}$* is the exact value answer*
> 
> **Final answer:** **0.764 rad (3 s.f.)**
> 
> (b) Convert $\frac{5π}{4}$ radians to degrees.
> 
> > *If you remember that *$\frac{π}{4}$* radians is 45°, then you just need to multiply that by 5 to get the answer.*
> 
> > *Otherwise, multiply by  *$\frac{180}{π}$
> 
> $\frac{5π}{4}\times\frac{180}{π}=\frac{5}{4}\times180=5\times45=225$
> 
> **Final answer:** **225°**

title: Linear Trigonometric Equations
bodyMd:
# Linear Trigonometric Equations

## Linear Trigonometric Equations

> **Spec point** — `10H`

## Linear Trigonometric Equations

### How do I solve trigonometric equations?

- **Trigonometric equations** can have an infinite number of solutions

  - For an equation in $\mathrm{sin}x$ or $\mathrm{cos}x$
  
    - you can **add or subtract 360°** (or **2*****π *****radians**) to each solution to find more solutions
  - For an equation in $\mathrm{tan}x$
  
    - you can **add or subtract 180°** (or ***π***** radians**) to each solution to find more solutions
- When **solving** a trigonometric equation

  - You will be given a **interval of values** within which the answers must lie
  
    - You need to find **all** the answers within that range
  - Using the inverse function on your calculator will only give you the **primary value**
  
    - This may or may not be in the required interval
  - The **other values** can be found with the help of:
  
    - your knowledge of trigonometric **exact values**
    - the **unit circle**
    - the **graphs of trigonometric functions**

### How are basic trigonometric equations solved?

- This means equations in the form  $\mathrm{sin}x=k$, $\mathrm{cos}x=k$  or  $\mathrm{tan}x=k$
- It can be helpful to **sketch the graph** of the trigonometric function first

  - Use the **given interval of values** as the domain for your graph
  - The **intersections** of the graph of the function and the line $y=k$ will show you
  
    - The **location** of the solutions
    - The **number** of solutions
  - You will be able to use the **symmetry** properties of the graph to find other values within the given interval

The methods for finding **all solutions** are:

- For the equation $\mathrm{sin}x=k$

  - The **primary value** is $x_{1}=\mathrm{sin}^{-1}k$
  - By symmetry, a **secondary value** is $x_{2}=180^{\circ}-\mathrm{sin}^{-1}k$
  
    - Either $x_{1}$ or $x_{2}$ might not actually be in the given interval!
  - Then **all values within the given interval** can be found using
  
    - $x_{1}\pm360n^{\circ}$
    - $x_{2}\pm360n^{\circ}$
    - where  $n=1,2,3,...$  as appropriate
- For the equation $\mathrm{cos}x=k$

  - The **primary value** is $x_{1}=\mathrm{cos}^{-1}k$
  - By symmetry, a **secondary value** is $x_{2}=-\mathrm{cos}^{-1}k$
  
    - Either $x_{1}$ or $x_{2}$ might not actually be in the given interval!
  - Then **all values within the given interval** can be found using
  
    - $x_{1}\pm360n^{\circ}$
    - $x_{2}\pm360n^{\circ}$
    - where  $n=1,2,3,...$  as appropriate
- For the equation $\mathrm{tan}x=k$

  - The **primary value** is $x_{1}=\mathrm{tan}^{-1}k$
  
    - $x_{1}$ might not actually be in the given interval!
  - Then **all values within the given interval** can be found using
  
    - $x\pm180n^{\circ}$
    - where  $n=1,2,3,...$  as appropriate

### How do I handle more complicated equations?

- You may need to use **algebra** to get an equation into one of the basic forms
- For example, $\mathrm{sin}x\mathrm{tan}x-3\mathrm{sin}x+\mathrm{tan}x=3$

  - **Subtract** 3 from both sides
  
    - $\mathrm{sin}x\mathrm{tan}x-3\mathrm{sin}x+\mathrm{tan}x-3=0$
  - **Factorise**
  
    - $\left(sin x + 1\right) \left(tan x - 3\right) = 0$
  - This gives you **two basic equations** to solve
  
    - $\mathrm{sin}x=-1$
    - $\mathrm{tan}x=3$
- Trigonometric **identities** and/or **addition formulae** may also be needed

> **Exam Hint**
> - Remember that your calculator will only give you the primary value
> 
>   - You need to be able to find all other solutions within the given interval
> - Sketching the trig graphs (or any other useful diagrams) can be a huge help!

> **Worked Example**
> Solve the equation  $2\mathrm{cos}x=-1$,  finding all solutions in the interval  $-2π\leqx\leq2π$.
> 
> *First isolate *$\mathrm{cos}x$
> 
> $\mathrm{cos}x=-\frac{1}{2}$
> 
> > *Use calculator or knowledge of exact trig values to find *$x_{1}$
> *Note that the interval is given in radians, so we must work in radians!*
> 
> $x_{1} = cos^{- 1} \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{2 \pi}{3}$
> 
> > *Use symmetry of the cos function to find *$x_{2}$
> 
> $x_{2}=-x_{1}=-\frac{2π}{3}$
> 
> > *Now add or subtract (multiples of) *$2π$* radians to find other solutions in the interval*
> 
> $x_{1}-2π=\frac{2π}{3}-2π=-\frac{4π}{3}$
> 
> $x_{2}+2π=-\frac{2π}{3}+2π=\frac{4π}{3}$
> 
> > *Any other additions or subtractions of *$2π$* would take us outside the interval*
> 
> $x=-\frac{4π}{3},-\frac{2π}{3},\frac{2π}{3},\frac{4π}{3}$

## Linear Trigonometric Equations (ax + b)

> **Spec point** — `10H`

## Linear Trigonometric Equations (ax + b)

### How can I solve equations with transformations of trig functions?

- This means equations of the form **sin(*****ax+b*****) = *****k***,  **cos(*****ax+b*****) = *****k***  or  **tan(*****ax+b*****) = *****k***

  - Trigonometric equations in these forms can be solved in **more than one way**
- The **easiest method** is to consider the transformation of the angle as a **substitution**

  - Let *u *= *ax *+ *b*
- **Transform the given interval** for the solutions in the same way as the angle

  - For example if the given interval is  0° ≤ x ≤ 360°  the new interval will be
  
    - (*a *(0°) + *b*) ≤ *u ≤ *(*a *(360°) + *b*)
- **Solve** the equation to find the **primary value** for *u*
- Find all the **other solutions** in the **transformed range** for *u*
- **Undo** the substitution

  - i.e.  $x=\frac{u-b}{a}$
  - Convert all of the *u *solutions back into corresponding solutions for *x*
- **Another method** would be to **sketch the transformation** of the function

  - If you use this method then you will not need to use a substitution for the range of values

> **Exam Hint**
> - If you use substitution and transform the interval
> 
>   - remember to convert answers back at the end!

> **Worked Example**
> Solve the equation  $2\mathrm{cos}(2x-30^{\circ})=-1$,  finding all solutions in the interval  $-360^{\circ}\leqx\leq360^{\circ}.$
> 
> > *We'll use the substitution  *$u=2x-30$
> 
> $\mathrm{Let}u=2x-30$
> 
> > *Rewrite the equation in terms of *$u$* and rearrange*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 cos u & = & - 1 \\ cos u & = & - \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Now we need to transform the interval as well*
> *Substitute the interval limits into  *$u=2x-30$
> 
> $2 \left(- 360\right) - 30 = - 750$
> 
> $2 \left(360\right) - 30 = 690$
> 
> $-750^{\circ}\lequ\leq690^{\circ}$
> 
> > *Use calculator or knowledge of exact trig values to find the primary value*
> 
> $u_{1} = cos^{- 1} \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) = 120$
> 
> > *Use symmetry of cos function to find the secondary value*
> 
> $u_{2}=-u_{1}=-120$
> 
> > *Sketch the graph of *$\mathrm{cos}u$* over the transformed interval*
> 
> ![cxVOKRsE_igcse-fpure-trig-eqns-we](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/b7cca12c61b9-cxvokrse-igcse-fpure-trig-eqns-we.png)
> 
> > *This shows that there are 8 places where *$\mathrm{cos}u=-\frac{1}{2}$
> 
> > *Find these by adding or subtracting (multiples of) *$360^{\circ}$* to *$u_{1}$* and *$u_{2}$
> 
> $u=-600,-480,-240,-120,120,240,480,600$
> 
> > *Invert the substitution*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}u & = & 2 x - 30 \\ 2 x & = & u + 30 \\ x & = & \frac{u + 30}{2}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Substitute the *$u$* values into  *$x=\frac{u+30}{2}$* to find the corresponding *$x$* values*
> 
> $x=-285^{\circ},-225^{\circ},-105^{\circ},-45^{\circ},75^{\circ},135^{\circ},255^{\circ},315^{\circ}$

title: Quadratic Trigonometric Equations
bodyMd:
# Quadratic Trigonometric Equations

## Quadratic Trigonometric Equations

> **Spec point** — `10H`

## Quadratic Trigonometric Equations

### How do I solve quadratic trigonometric equations?

- A **quadratic trigonometric equation** is one that includes either $\mathrm{sin}^{2}x$, $\mathrm{cos}^{2}x$ or $\mathrm{tan}^{2}x$
- Often the **identity**$\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ+\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ=1$ can be used to help solve the equation

  - This can change an equation with **both** sine and cosine
  - into an equation with **only** sine **or** cosine
- Solve the **quadratic equation **using any of the usual methods

  - You may find it easier to **rewrite** it as an equation with a single letter
  
    - e.g. writing  $2\mathrm{cos}^{2}x+5\mathrm{cos}x-3=0$  as  $2c^{2}+5c-3=0$
- A quadratic can give **up to two** solutions

  - You must check whether solutions to the quadratic are **valid** solutions
  
    - $\left(2 cos\right)^{2}  x + 5 cos  x - 3 = \left(2 cos x - 1\right) \left(cos x + 3\right) = 0$
    - So $\mathrm{cos}x=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\mathrm{cos}x=-3$ are the solutions of the quadratic
  - Remember that solutions for $\mathrm{sin}x=k$ and $\mathrm{cos}x=k$ **only exist** for $-1\leqk\leq1$
  
    - So $\mathrm{cos}x=-3$ may be a correct solution for the quadratic
    - But it does not give a valid solution for the trigonometric equation!
  - Solutions for $\mathrm{tan}x=k$ exist for **all** values of $k$
- After you solve the **quadratic equation**

  - Find all solutions for the resulting **trigonometric equation(s)** within the given interval
  
    - For the example above this would mean solving $\mathrm{cos}x=\frac{1}{2}$
  - There will often be **more than two** trigonometric solutions for one quadratic equation
  - **Sketching a graph** can help check how many solutions there should be in the given interval

> **Exam Hint**
> - Sketch the trig graphs on your exam paper
> 
>   - Then you can refer back to them as many times as you need to
> - Make sure you have found **all** of the solutions in the given interval
> 
>   - And that you don't give solutions outside the interval
>   - For example if you get a negative solution but the interval is entirely positive

> **Worked Example**
> Solve the equation $11\mathrm{sin}x--7=5\mathrm{cos}^{2}x$, finding all solutions in the interval  $0\leqx\leq2π$.  Give your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
> 
> > $\mathrm{sin}^{2}x+\mathrm{cos}^{2}x=1$*  can be rearranged as  *$\mathrm{cos}^{2}x=1-\mathrm{sin}^{2}x$
> 
> > *Substitute this to get the equation entirely in terms of *$\mathrm{sin}x$
> 
> $11 sin x - 7 = 5 \left(1 - sin^{2} x\right)$
> 
> > *Expand the brackets and rearrange to get a quadratic equal to zero*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}11 sin x - 7 & = & 5 - 5 sin^{2} x \\ 5 sin^{2} x + 11 sin x - 12 & = & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *This can be solved by factorising (it might help you to think of it as  *$5s^{2}+11s-12=0$*)*
> *You could also solve it by using the quadratic formula*
> *Or your calculator may be able to solve quadratics*
> 
> $( 5 \text{sin} x - 4 ) ( \text{sin} x + 3 ) = 0$
> 
> sin x equals 4 over 5 space space or space space sin x equals negative 3
> 
> > $\mathrm{sin}x=-3$*  has no solutions for *$x$* because sine cannot be less than *$-1$
> *So we only need to find solutions for *$\mathrm{sin}x=\frac{4}{5}$
> 
> > *Start by finding the primary solution*
> *The interval is given in radians, so we have to make sure the calculator is set up for radians!*
> 
> $x_{1} = sin^{- 1} \left(\frac{4}{5}\right) = 0 . 927295 . . .$
> 
> > *Use symmetry properties of sine to find the secondary solution*
> 
> $x_{2} = \pi - x_{1} = \pi - sin^{- 1} \left(\frac{4}{5}\right) = 2 . 214297 . . .$
> 
> > *Both those solutions are the interval *$0\leqx\leq2π$*, and there are no other solutions in the interval*
> *(You could sketch the sine function to confirm that)*
> 
> $x=0.927,2.21(3s.f.)$

title: Sine & Cosine Formulae
bodyMd:
# Sine & Cosine Formulae

## Sine Formula

> **Spec point** — `10D`

## Sine Formula

### What is the sine formula?

- The **sine formula** allows us to find missing side lengths or angles in **non**-**right-angled triangles**

  - It is also known as the **sine rule**
- It states that for **any triangle** with angles *A, B* and *C*

  - $\frac{a}{\mathrm{sin}A}=\frac{b}{\mathrm{sin}B}=\frac{c}{\mathrm{sin}C}$

- *a *is the side **opposite** angle *A*
- *b *is the side **opposite** angle *B*
- *c *is the side **opposite** angle *C*
- This formula is **not** on the exam formula sheet, so you need to remember it
- Remember that sin 90° = 1

  - So if one of the angles is 90° this becomes SOH from** SOHCAHTOA**

![Labelling a triangle with A, B, C and a, b, c](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/74ea68ddea24-5-1-3-non-right-angled-triangles-diagram-1a.png)

### How can I use the sine formula to find missing side lengths or angles?

- The sine formula can be used when you have any **opposite pairs** of sides and angles
- Always **start by labelling your triangle** with the angles and sides

  - Remember
  
    - the sides with the lower-case letters
    - are **opposite** the angles with the equivalent upper-case letters
- Use the formula as given above to find the **length of a side**
- To find a **missing angle** it's easier to 'flip' the formula

  - $\frac{\mathrm{sin}A}{a}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}B}{b}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}C}{c}$

- **Substitute** the values you have into the formula and solve

  - This will always give you an **acute** angle
  - If you know the angle is **obtuse** then subtract this value from 180

> **Exam Hint**
> - Remember to check that your calculator is in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians)!

> **Worked Example**
> The following diagram shows triangle $ABC$.  $AB=8.1\mathrm{cm}$, $BC=12.3\mathrm{cm}$, and angle $BCA=27^{\circ}$. It is also given that angle $BAC$ is acute.
> 
> ![3-3-2-sine-rule-we-question](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/0982c6ee3f6d-3-3-2-sine-rule-we-question.png)
> 
> (a) Find the value of $x$,
> 
> ![3-3-2-ai-sl-sine-rule-we-solution-i](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/4363f94a8100-3-3-2-ai-sl-sine-rule-we-solution-i.png)
> 
> (b) Find the value of $y$.
> 
> ![3-3-2-ai-sl-sine-rule-we-solution-ii](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/d47dc25e2e15-3-3-2-ai-sl-sine-rule-we-solution-ii.png)

## Cosine Formula

> **Spec point** — `10D`

## Cosine Formula

### What is the cosine formula?

- The cosine formula allows us to find missing side lengths or angles in **non**-**right-angled triangles**

  - It is also known as the **cosine rule**
- It states that for **any triangle**

  - $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\mathrm{cos}A$

- *a *is the side **opposite** angle *A*
- *b *and *c *are the **other two sides**
- angle *A* is the angle **in between** sides *b* and *c*
- This formula is on the exam **formula sheet**

  - So you don't need to remember it
  - But you do need to be able to use it
- Remember cos 90° = 0

  - So if A = 90° this becomes **Pythagoras’ Theorem**

### How can I use the cosine formula to find missing side lengths or angles?

- The cosine rule can be used when you have **two sides and the angle between them** or **all three sides**
- Always **start by labelling your triangle** with the angles and sides

  - Remember
  
    - the sides with the lower-case letters
    - are **opposite** the angles with the equivalent upper-case letters
- Use the formula in the formula sheet form to find an **unknown side**
- **Rearrange** the formula to find an **unknown angle**

  - $\mathrm{cos}A=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2bc}$
  
    - Remember, *A *must be the angle **in between** sides *b *and c
- **Substitute** the values you have into the formula and solve

> **Exam Hint**
> - Remember to check that your calculator is in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians)!

> **Worked Example**
> The following diagram shows triangle $ABC$. $AB=4.2\mathrm{km}$, $BC=3.8\mathrm{km}$, and $AC=7.1\mathrm{km}$.
> 
> ![3-3-2-cosine-rule-we-question](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/8b9f9c95cda8-3-3-2-cosine-rule-we-question.png)
> 
> Calculate the size of angle $ABC$.
> 
> ![4-11-1-cosine-rule-new-we-solution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/9abe05ffa3a2-4-11-1-cosine-rule-new-we-solution.png)

## Area of a Triangle

> **Spec point** — `10D`

## Area of a Triangle

### How do I find the area of a non-right-angled triangle?

- The area of **any triangle** can be found using the formula

  - $\mathrm{Area}=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$
  
    - *C *is the angle **in between** sides *a *and *b*
  - This formula is **not** on the exam formula sheet, so you need to remember it
- Remember sin 90° = 1

  - so **if C = 90°** this becomes Area = ½ × base × height
- If you know the **area** you can use the formula to find the **length of a side** or an **angle**

  - Using inverse sin will always give you an **acute** angle
  
    - Subtract the value from 180 if you know the angle is **obtuse**

> **Exam Hint**
> - Be careful to label your triangle correctly
> 
>   - so that your angle *C* is always the angle between the two sides
> - Remember to check that your calculator is in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians)!

> **Worked Example**
> The following diagram shows triangle $ABC$. $AB=32\mathrm{cm}$, $AC=1.1m$, and angle $BAC=74^{\circ}$.
> 
> ![3-3-2-area-rule-we-question](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/71f5a10c245a-3-3-2-area-rule-we-question.png)
> 
> Calculate the area of triangle, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
> 
> ![3-3-2-ai-sl-area-rule-we-solution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-further-maths-19/assets/96655e6bf616-3-3-2-ai-sl-area-rule-we-solution.png)

title: Trigonometric Addition Formulae
bodyMd:
# Trigonometric Addition Formulae

## Trigonometric Addition Formulae

> **Spec point** — `10G`

## Trigonometric Addition Formulae

### What are the trigonometric addition formulae?

- There are six **trigonometric addition formulae** (also known as **compound angle formulae**),

  - two each for **sin**, **cos** and **tan**
- The formulae for **sin** are

  - $sin \left(A + B\right) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B$
  - $sin \left(A - B\right) = sin A cos B - cos A sin B$
  
    - Note that the +/- sign on the left-hand side **matches** the one on the right-hand side

- The formulae for **cos** are

  - $cos \left(A + B\right) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B$
  - $cos \left(A - B\right) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B$
  
    - Note that the +/- sign on the left-hand side is **opposite to** the one on the right-hand side

- The formulae for **tan** are

  - $tan \left(A + B\right)  \equiv \frac{tan A + tan B}{1 - tan A tan B}$
  - $tan \left(A - B\right)  \equiv \frac{tan A - tan B}{1 + tan A tan B}$
  
    - Note that the +/- sign on the left-hand side **matches** the one in the **numerator** on the right-hand side, and is **opposite to** the one in the **denominator**
- These formulae are all on the **exam formula sheet**

  - so you don't need to remember them
  - but you do need to be able to use them

### What are the double angle formulae?

- The **double angle formulae** are special cases of the trigonometric addition formulae

  - They are formed by setting $A=B$ in the '+' versions of the addition formulae
- The **sin** version is

  - $sin \left(2 A\right) = 2 sin A cos A$
- The **cos** version is

  - $cos \left(2 A\right) = cos^{2} A - sin^{2} A = 1 - 2 sin^{2} A = 2 cos^{2} A - 1$
  
    - The last two forms come from using the $\mathrm{sin}^{2}A+\mathrm{cos}^{2}A=1$ identity
    - i.e. $\mathrm{cos}^{2}A=1-\mathrm{sin}^{2}A$ and $\mathrm{sin}^{2}A=1-\mathrm{cos}^{2}A$
- The **tan** version is

  - $tan \left(2 A\right) = \frac{2 tan A}{1 - tan^{2} A}$
- These formulae are **not** on the exam formula sheet

  - They are used frequently, so you may want to remember them
  - But they are also easy to derive from the addition formulae that are on the sheet

### How are the trigonometric addition formulae used?

- The formulae can be used to find the **values** of trigonometric ratios **without a calculator**

  - For example, to find the value of sin15°
  
    - **rewrite** it as sin(45–30)°
    - apply the **formula** for sin(A –B)
    - use your knowledge of **exact values** to calculate the answer
- The formulae can also be used

  - to **derive** further trigonometric identities (like the double angle formulae)
  - in trigonometric **proof**
  - to **simplify** trigonometric equations before solving

> **Exam Hint**
> - Remember that the trigonometric addition formulae are on the exam formula sheet
> 
>   - But always be careful with the +/- signs when using the formulae

> **Worked Example**
> a) Show that $tan \left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) -  tan \left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{2 \left(tan^{2} x + 1\right)}{1 - tan^{2} x}$.
> 
> > *Use the trigonometric addition formulae for tan*
> 
> > *Also recall that *$\mathrm{tan}\frac{π}{4}=1$
> 
> $tan \left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{tan x + tan \frac{\pi}{4}}{1 - tan x tan \frac{\pi}{4}} = \frac{tan x + 1}{1 - tan x}$
> 
> $tan \left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{tan x - tan \frac{\pi}{4}}{1 + tan x tan \frac{\pi}{4}} = \frac{tan x - 1}{1 + tan x}$
> 
> > *Substitute those into the left-hand side of the equation and rearrange*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}tan \left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) - tan \left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) & = & \frac{tan x + 1}{1 - tan x} - \frac{tan x - 1}{1 + tan x} \\ & = & \frac{\left(tan x + 1\right) \left(1 + tan x\right) - \left(tan x - 1\right) \left(1 - tan x\right)}{\left(1 - tan x\right) \left(1 + tan x\right)} \\ & = & \frac{tan^{2} x + 2 tan x + 1 + tan^{2} x - 2 tan x + 1}{1 - tan^{2} x} \\ & = & \frac{2 tan^{2} x + 2}{1 - tan^{2} x} \\ & = & \frac{2 \left(tan^{2} x + 1\right)}{1 - tan^{2} x}\end{aligned}$
> 
> $\mathbf{tan} \left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) -  \mathbf{tan} \left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{2 \left(\mathbf{tan}^{2} \mathbf{x} + 1\right)}{1 - \mathbf{tan}^{2} \mathbf{x}}$
> 
> b) Hence solve $ tan \left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) - tan \left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = - 4$  in the interval  $0\leqx\leq\frac{π}{2}$.
> 
> *Substitute the result from part (a) into the equation*
> 
> > *Then rearrange and solve*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}\frac{2 \left(tan^{2} x + 1\right)}{1 - tan^{2} x} & = & - 4 \\ \frac{tan^{2} x + 1}{1 - tan^{2} x} & = & - 2 \\ tan^{2} x + 1 & = & 2 tan^{2} x - 2 \\ tan^{2} x & = & 3 \\ tan x & = & \pm \sqrt{3} \\ x & = & \frac{\pi}{3} ,  - \frac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *But only *$\frac{π}{3}$* is in the range *$0\leqx\leq\frac{π}{2}$
> 
> $x=\frac{π}{3}$

title: Trigonometric Identities
bodyMd:
# Trigonometric Identities

## Trigonometric Identities

> **Spec point** — `10E`

## Trigonometric Identities

### What is a trigonometric identity?

- **Trigonometric identities** are statements about **trigonometric functions** like $\mathrm{sin}θ$, $\mathrm{cos}θ$ and $\mathrm{tan}θ$

  - They are **true** for **all values** of the angle $θ$
  - They can be used to help **simplify** trigonometric equations before solving them
- Sometimes you may see identities written with the **symbol ** $\equiv$  instead of an equals sign

  - This means 'identical to' or 'equivalent to'

### What trigonometric identities do I need to know?

- You must know these **two trigonometric identities**:

  - $\mathrm{tan}θ=\frac{\mathrm{sin}θ}{\mathrm{cos}θ}$
  
    - This is the identity for $\mathrm{tan}θ$
  - $\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ+\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ=1$
  
    - This is sometimes called the Pythagorean identity
    - Note that the notation $\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ$ is the same thing as $(\mathrm{sin}θ)^{2}$
- The second identity is often used in one of its **rearranged forms**

  - $\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ=1-\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ$
  - $\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ=1-\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ$

> **Exam Hint**
> - When asked to show that one thing is equal or identical to another, look at what parts are 'missing'
> 
>   - This can help you spot which identity to use

> **Worked Example**
> Show that the equation $2\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ-\mathrm{cos}θ=0$ can be written in the form  $a\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ+b\mathrm{cos}θ+c=0$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers to be found with $a>0$.
> 
> > *Note that in the 'target' form there is no *$\mathrm{sin}θ$* or *$\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ$
> 
> > *That means we want to use a substitution to get rid of the *$\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ$* in the original form*
> 
> > *We can do this using the identity *$\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ+\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ=1$*, rearranged as  *$\mathrm{sin}^{2}θ=1-\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 sin^{2} \theta - cos \theta & = & 2 \left(1  -  cos^{2} \theta\right) - cos \theta \\ & = & 2 - 2 cos^{2} \theta - cos \theta \\ & = & - 2 cos^{2} \theta - cos \theta + 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Substitute that back into the original equation*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}- 2 cos^{2} \theta - cos \theta + 2 & = & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Multiply both sides of the equation by *$-1$* to make the *$\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ$* coefficient positive*
> 
> > *This gets the equation into the required form with  *$a=2$*, *$b=1$* and *$c=-2$
> 
> $2\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ+\mathrm{cos}θ-2=0$

# Basic Trigonometry

## Right-Angled Trigonometry

> **Spec point** — `10B`

## Right-Angled Trigonometry

### What is right-angled trigonometry?

- **Right-angled trigonometry** is the study of right-angled triangles

  - In particular the relationships between their **side lengths** and **angles**
- Right-angled trigonometry includes** two **main components

  - The **Pythagorean theorem**
  - **SOHCAHTOA**
- You should **already** be familiar with right-angled trigonometry from your regular IGCSE Mathematics course

### What is the Pythagorean theorem?

- The **Pythagorean theorem** (or Pythagoras’ theorem ) connects the side lengths in a right-angled triangle

  - It **only** works for right-angled triangles!
- It says that for any right-angled triangle, the **square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides**

  - The **hypotenuse **is always the **longest side** in a right-angled triangle
  
    - It will always be **opposite** the right angle
- If we **label** the hypotenuse *c*, and label the other two sides *a* and *b*, then

  - $c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}$
  
    - This is **not** on the exam formula sheet, so you need to remember it
- This lets us **find one side length** if we know the other two side lengths

  - To find the hypotenuse
